cards.a: Left-hand limit 3, right-hand limit 3, two-sided limit 3, and g(1) = −1. From both sides the curve's height approaches the open circle at height 3, so the one-sided limits agree and the limit is 3; the filled dot gives the function value, which does not affect the limit.
cards.h: → four values, then which feature gives which
cards.n: Using the filled dot for the limit (answering −1) is the classic misreading: filled dots give values, the curve's approach gives limits.

cards.q: Determine the two one-sided limits and $\lim_{x \to 2} k(x)$ when the graph of k falls without bound as x approaches 2 from the left and rises without bound as x approaches 2 from the right (x = 2 is a vertical asymptote).
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} k(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} k(x) = \infty$, so $\lim_{x \to 2} k(x)$ does not exist. Neither one-sided limit is a real number, because k is unbounded; −∞ and ∞ describe the direction. Since the two sides even head in opposite directions, not even ±∞ describes the two-sided behavior.
cards.h: → two one-sided results, then the two-sided verdict
cards.n: Writing 'the limit is ∞' for the two-sided limit is wrong twice: the sides disagree, and ∞ is never a real limit value.

cards.q: Explain what a standard graphing-calculator window hides about $y = \frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ near x = 2, and why limits read from a graph are estimates.
cards.a: The screen shows an unbroken line y = x + 2, but the function is undefined at x = 2: the graph has a one-point hole at (2, 4), narrower than a pixel. The picture correctly suggests the limit 4 but hides the discontinuity. Because of scale, a graph can miss holes, tiny jumps or rapid oscillation, so a value read from a graph is an estimate to be confirmed analytically.
cards.h: → what is hidden, then why graphs only estimate
cards.n: 'The calculator shows f(2) = 4' is false: evaluating at x = 2 gives an error; the picture simply cannot show a single missing point.

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist when the graph of f approaches height 2 from the left of x = 2 and height 5 from the right.
cards.a: A two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal. Here $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = 2$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = 5$; since 2 ≠ 5, the values of f do not approach a single number, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist.
cards.h: → left limit 2 → right limit 5 → 2 ≠ 5 → no single value approached → DNE
cards.n: Averaging to 3.5, or quoting the side that f(2) belongs to, earns nothing; name both one-sided limits and state that they are unequal.
o: The graph has a jump at x = 2: points just to the left have heights near 2 and points just to the right have heights near 5, so no single height is approached.
If the limit were some L, both one-sided limits would equal L, forcing 2 = L = 5, which is impossible.

w.a: The limit is 3.5, halfway between the two sides.
w.why: a limit is not an average of the one-sided limits

w.a: The limit does not exist because f(2) is undefined.
w.why: f(2) plays no part in whether the limit exists

w.a: The limit is 5 because the graph is higher on the right.
w.why: one side alone does not determine a two-sided limit

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to 0} \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$ does not exist even though the function is bounded between −1 and 1.
cards.a: Bounded is not enough: a limit needs the values to approach one number. As x → 0, 1/x grows without bound, so sin(1/x) keeps cycling through every value in [−1, 1]; it equals 1 and −1 at points arbitrarily close to 0, so no single value L is approached.
cards.h: → 1/x → ∞ → sine keeps cycling → hits 1 and −1 arbitrarily near 0 → no single value
cards.n: 'It doesn't exist because 1/0 is undefined' earns nothing: sin(x)/x is also undefined at 0, yet its limit is 1.
o: Along x = 2/((4k + 1)π) the values are all 1 and along x = 2/((4k + 3)π) they are all −1; approaching two different values means there is no limit.
The graph oscillates infinitely often in every interval around 0, which is the oscillation failure mode, not a jump or unboundedness.

w.a: The limit is 0 because sine averages out to zero.
w.why: an average value is not a limit

w.a: The limit does not exist because sin(1/0) is undefined.
w.why: being undefined at the point says nothing about the limit

w.a: The limit is ∞ because 1/x goes to infinity.
w.why: sine of a huge input still stays between −1 and 1

cards.q: Explain why a limit value read from a graph should be treated as an estimate.
cards.a: A graph shows f at a limited scale: a one-point hole, a tiny jump, or oscillation faster than the pixels can resolve may be invisible, and heights can only be read approximately. So the graph suggests a value, and the limit should be confirmed analytically with algebra or limit theorems.
cards.h: → finite scale → holes, tiny jumps, oscillation can hide → readings are approximate → confirm analytically
cards.n: 'Graphs are exact if you zoom in far enough' misses it: no zoom level shows a single missing point or proves a value.
o: Different functions such as (x² − 4)/(x − 2) and x + 2 can produce identical-looking graphs yet differ at x = 2, so the picture cannot settle every question about the point.
A reading such as 'about 3' from gridlines is only as precise as the gridline spacing; the exact value needs the formula.

w.a: A graph gives the exact limit as long as it is drawn by a calculator.
w.why: calculator pixels can hide holes and fine behavior

w.a: Graphs are only estimates because you might misread the function value at the point.
w.why: the limit does not use the function value at the point

cards.q: Explain how to estimate a limit from a table of values, and the caution required.
cards.a: Choose x-values approaching a from both sides (such as a − 0.1, a − 0.01, a − 0.001 and a + 0.001, a + 0.01, a + 0.1), read the f(x) values in each direction, and see whether both trends settle toward the same number; that number is the estimate. Caution: a table only suggests a limit. Finitely many values cannot prove it exists, and badly chosen x-values can mislead.
cards.n: Claiming the table 'proves' the limit, or reading only one side, loses the point; word the result as an estimate: the values appear to approach L.

cards.a: About 6. From the left, 5.7 and 5.97 increase toward 6; from the right, 6.3 and 6.03 decrease toward 6. Both one-sided trends point to the same value, so the table suggests $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 6$. The data fit f(x) = 3x, but the table alone does not prove that.
cards.h: → one value, with both one-sided trends
cards.n: Answering 'f(2) = 6' makes a different claim: the table has no entry at x = 2, and a limit estimate says nothing about f(2).

cards.q: A table gives f(2.9) = 7.8, f(2.99) = 7.98, f(3.01) = -7.98, f(3.1) = -7.8. Decide whether $\lim_{x \to 3} f(x)$ exists based on this data, and explain.
cards.a: It appears not to exist. From the left the values 7.8, 7.98 approach 8, so the left-hand limit appears to be 8; from the right the values −7.8, −7.98 approach −8. The one-sided limits appear unequal, so the two-sided limit appears not to exist, consistent with a jump at x = 3.
cards.n: Averaging the sides to get 0, or quoting only one side, earns nothing; compare the two one-sided trends explicitly.

cards.q:
Estimate $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} g(x)$ for g(x) = x^x, which is defined only for x > 0, from this table, and explain why only a one-sided limit is asked.
x · g(x)
0.1 · 0.7943
0.01 · 0.9550
0.001 · 0.9931
0.0001 · 0.9991
cards.a: About 1. As x decreases toward 0 through positive values, g(x) rises 0.7943, 0.9550, 0.9931, 0.9991, closing in on 1, so $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} x^{x}$ appears to be 1. Only the right-hand limit makes sense because g is undefined for x < 0, so there are no values on the left to read.
cards.h: → one value from the trend, then the domain reason
cards.n: Guessing 0 ('0 to any power is 0') or 1 ('anything to the 0 is 1') is not an estimate; the form 0⁰ is indeterminate and only the trend supports 1.

cards.a: The values grow without bound from both sides, so the limit appears not to exist as a real number; the behavior is described by $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = \infty$. Each step ten times closer to 1 multiplies f(x) by 100 with no leveling off, which suggests a vertical asymptote at x = 1 (the data match 1/(x − 1)²).
cards.h: → verdict, then the pattern in the values
cards.n: Estimating 'about 1,000,000' reports the last entry, not a limit; unbounded growth means no real-number limit exists.

cards.q: Represent $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{x}-1}{x}$ numerically: make a table of values at x = ±0.1, ±0.01, ±0.001 (calculator, 4 decimal places) and use it to estimate the limit.
cards.a:
x · (e^x − 1)/x
−0.1 · 0.9516
−0.01 · 0.9950
−0.001 · 0.9995
0.001 · 1.0005
0.01 · 1.0050
0.1 · 1.0517
Estimate: 1. The left-side values rise toward 1 and the right-side values fall toward 1.
cards.n: Evaluating at x = 0 gives 0/0, which tells nothing; the table must use x ≠ 0 from both sides (Unit 2 shows the value is exactly 1).

cards.a: About 2.718. From the left the values decrease 2.73200, 2.71964, 2.71842, and from the right they increase 2.70481, 2.71692, 2.71815, trapping the limit between 2.71815 and 2.71842; both round to 2.718. (The limit is the number e ≈ 2.71828.)
cards.h: → bracket from both sides, then round
cards.n: Rounding one side's last entry alone (2.717 from x = 0.001) misses the third decimal; the two-sided bracket is what justifies 2.718.

cards.q: Estimate $\lim_{x \to 3} h(x)$ from the table h(2.9) = 4.1, h(2.99) = 4.01, h(3) = 10, h(3.01) = 3.99, h(3.1) = 3.9, and state what the entry h(3) = 10 contributes.
cards.a: The limit appears to be 4. From the left (4.1, 4.01) and from the right (3.9, 3.99) the values close in on 4. The entry h(3) = 10 contributes nothing to the limit, which uses only x ≠ 3; together with the estimate it suggests a removable discontinuity at x = 3 (limit 4, value 10).
cards.h: → estimate, then the role of the entry at x = 3
cards.n: Answering 10 because it is the table's value at x = 3 is the trap; the limit is read from the neighbors, never from the point.

cards.q: Explain why a table of values can suggest a limit but cannot prove it, using f(x) = sin(π/x) at x = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
cards.a: A table shows finitely many values. At x = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 the values sin(10π), sin(100π), sin(1000π) are all 0, suggesting a limit of 0; but at x = 2/401 ≈ 0.005 the value is sin(200.5π) = 1, and f oscillates between −1 and 1 near 0, so the limit does not exist.
cards.h: → finitely many samples → the samples all land on zeros → other inputs give 1 → the limit DNE
cards.n: 'The table shows 0, 0, 0, so the limit is 0' is exactly the error; the samples happened to line up with special points.
o: Only an analytic argument (algebra, a theorem, continuity) covers every x near 0; a table covers a handful of inputs.
Choosing x = 2/(4k + 1) instead gives values of 1 every time, contradicting the pattern of zeros.

w.a: The table proves the limit is 0 because every value is exactly 0.
w.why: finitely many samples cannot rule out other behavior

w.a: The limit is 0 because the sine of a multiple of π is always 0.
w.why: π/x is a whole multiple of π only at special x

w.a: Tables never give useful information about limits.
w.why: they give evidence; they just do not prove

cards.q: Explain why values from both sides of x = a must be examined when estimating $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ from a table.
cards.a: The two-sided limit exists only if the left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are equal. Values with x < a estimate only the left-hand limit; the right side could approach a different value (a jump) or be unbounded, so both sides must show the same trend before one limit is claimed.
cards.h: → two-sided limit needs both one-sided limits → one side can hide a jump → check both
cards.n: 'The left side approaches 8, so the limit is 8' earns nothing unless the right side is shown to agree.
o: Values with x > a estimate the right-hand limit; only when both estimates agree does the table suggest a two-sided limit.
For |x − a|/(x − a) the left values are all −1 and the right values all 1; reading one side would give a wrong limit.

w.a: You only need one side because a function behaves the same on both sides.
w.why: piecewise functions and jumps break that

w.a: Checking both sides is only needed when f(a) is undefined.
w.why: f(a) is irrelevant; the one-sided limits can differ either way

cards.q: Explain why the table entry h(3) = 10 does not change the estimate of $\lim_{x \to 3} h(x)$ when the nearby values approach 4.
cards.a: A limit is determined by the values of h(x) for x close to 3 but not equal to 3. The entries at 2.9, 2.99, 3.01, 3.1 approach 4, so the limit appears to be 4; the value at x = 3 is excluded by the definition, so h(3) = 10 shows only that h is not continuous there.
cards.h: → the limit uses x ≠ 3 → the neighbors approach 4 → h(3) is excluded → limit 4, h discontinuous
cards.n: 'The limit is 10 because the table gives it directly' confuses the value at the point with the value approached.
o: The picture is a removable discontinuity: a hole at height 4 with the point plotted at height 10.
Changing h(3) to any other number leaves every value the limit uses unchanged, so the limit cannot depend on it.

w.a: The limit is 10 because that is the actual value at 3.
w.why: the limit never uses the value at the point

w.a: The limit does not exist because h(3) disagrees with the other values.
w.why: that disagreement breaks continuity, not the limit

w.a: The limit is 7, the average of 4 and 10.
w.why: a limit is not an average

cards.q: State the limit laws for sums, constant multiples, products, and quotients.
cards.a: If $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = M$ both exist, then lim(f ± g) = L ± M; lim(c·f) = cL; lim(f·g) = LM; and lim(f/g) = L/M provided M ≠ 0. Also lim [f(x)]ⁿ = Lⁿ for a positive integer n.
cards.n: Every law needs both limits to exist first; splitting a limit when one part does not exist, or using the quotient law with M = 0, is the classic error.

cards.q: Explain when direct substitution is guaranteed to produce a limit.
cards.a: When f is continuous at a: then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. Polynomials are continuous everywhere, and rational, power, exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions are continuous at every point of their domains, so for these, substituting an x-value in the domain gives the limit.
cards.h: → one condition, then which function families
cards.n: If substitution gives 0/0, that is neither an answer nor a DNE; it only signals that an equivalent expression is needed.

cards.q: Given $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$ and $\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = -3$, compute $\lim_{x \to 2}\left[2f(x) - 3g(x)\right]$.
cards.a: 19. Both limits exist, so the difference and constant-multiple laws give $\lim_{x \to 2}[2f(x) - 3g(x)] = 2\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) - 3\lim_{x \to 2} g(x) = 2(5) - 3(-3) = 10 + 9 = 19$.
cards.h: → split by the laws, then substitute
cards.n: The sign slip: 2(5) − 3(−3) is 10 + 9, not 10 − 9 = 1; subtracting a negative adds.

cards.q: Given $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 4$ and $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = 2$, compute $\lim_{x \to 1}\left[\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} + f(x)g(x)\right]$.
cards.a: 10. Both limits exist and $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = 2 \ne 0$, so the quotient law gives 4/2 = 2, the product law gives 4·2 = 8, and the sum law gives 2 + 8 = 10.
cards.n: The quotient law needs lim g(x) ≠ 0; check it (here 2 ≠ 0) before dividing, or the step is unjustified.

cards.q:
Evaluate each limit by direct substitution, valid because each function is continuous at the point.
1. $\lim_{x \to 3} (2x^{2} - x + 4)$
2. $\lim_{x \to -1} \frac{x^{3}+2}{x-2}$
3. $\lim_{x \to \pi} x\cos x$
4. $\lim_{x \to 0} (e^{x} + \sin x)$
5. $\lim_{x \to 4} \sqrt{2x+1}$
6. $\lim_{x \to e} \ln\left(x^{2}\right)$
7. $\lim_{x \to \pi/4} \tan x$
8. $\lim_{x \to 2} \left(x^{2}+1\right)^{3}$
9. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos x - 1}{x+1}$
10. $\lim_{x \to -2} |x-3|$
11. $\lim_{x \to 3} 2^{x}$
12. $\lim_{x \to 1/2} \frac{1}{\sin(\pi x)}$
cards.n: Substitution is justified by continuity at the point, not by habit; item 9 looks like a trig 0/0 form, but its denominator approaches 1.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 2} \sqrt{x^{2}+5}$ and name the limit theorem that justifies the step inside the root.
cards.a: 3. By the limit of a composite function: $\lim_{x \to 2} (x^{2}+5) = 9$ and the square-root function is continuous at 9, so $\lim_{x \to 2} \sqrt{x^{2}+5} = \sqrt{\lim_{x \to 2}(x^{2}+5)} = \sqrt{9} = 3$.
cards.n: Moving a limit inside an outer function needs that outer function to be continuous at the inner limit; without that the step is unjustified.

cards.q: Determine $\lim_{x \to 1} f(g(x))$, given that g(x) → 2 as x → 1 with g(x) > 2 for all x ≠ 1 near 1, and that $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = 5$, $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = -1$, and f(2) = 0.
cards.a: −1. As x → 1 from either side, the inputs g(x) approach 2 from above, since g(x) > 2. So f(g(x)) behaves like f(u) as u → 2⁺, and $\lim_{x \to 1} f(g(x)) = \lim_{u \to 2^{+}} f(u) = -1$. Neither f(2) = 0 nor the left-hand limit 5 is used.
cards.h: → direction of the inner approach, then that side of f
cards.n: Answering f(2) = 0, or 'DNE because f jumps at 2', ignores that g feeds f only inputs above 2.

cards.q: Determine $\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} f(x)$, $\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} f(x)$, and $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x)$ for f(x) = x² + 1 when x < 1 and f(x) = 3x − 1 when x ≥ 1.
cards.a: Left: $\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} (x^{2}+1) = 2$. Right: $\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} (3x - 1) = 2$. The one-sided limits are equal, so $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2$. Each side uses the formula that holds on that side, and each piece is a polynomial, so substitution is valid within its piece.
cards.h: → each side with its own piece, then compare
cards.n: Evaluating only the x ≥ 1 piece because 'x = 1 belongs to it' gives the right-hand limit alone; the left side needs x² + 1.

cards.q: Determine $\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} \frac{x^{2}-9}{|x-3|}$ and $\lim_{x \to 3^{+}} \frac{x^{2}-9}{|x-3|}$, and state whether the two-sided limit exists.
cards.a: The left-hand limit is −6 and the right-hand limit is 6, so the two-sided limit does not exist. For x < 3, |x − 3| = −(x − 3), so the quotient is (x − 3)(x + 3)/(−(x − 3)) = −(x + 3) → −6. For x > 3, |x − 3| = x − 3, so the quotient is x + 3 → 6.
cards.h: → rewrite |x − 3| on each side, cancel, compare
cards.n: Treating |x − 3| as x − 3 on both sides gives 6 twice; for x < 3 the absolute value flips the sign.

cards.q: Determine $\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x) + g(x)]$ and $\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x) g(x)]$, or explain why one does not exist, when at x = 0 f has left-hand limit 1 and right-hand limit 3, and g has left-hand limit 2 and right-hand limit 0.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x) + g(x)] = 3$: from the left 1 + 2 = 3 and from the right 3 + 0 = 3, so the one-sided limits agree. $\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x)g(x)]$ does not exist: from the left 1·2 = 2, from the right 3·0 = 0, and 2 ≠ 0. The laws are applied one side at a time because f and g have only one-sided limits.
cards.h: → combine one side at a time, then compare the sides
cards.n: 'Neither f nor g has a limit, so the sum cannot have one' is false; the laws need existence to split a limit, but a sum can exist without its parts.

cards.q: Explain why the quotient law cannot be used to evaluate $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}$.
cards.a: The quotient law requires the limit of the denominator to be nonzero. Here $\lim_{x \to 3} (x - 3) = 0$, so the hypothesis fails, and lim(top)/lim(bottom) would be 0/0, which is not a value. The expression must be rewritten first: for x ≠ 3 it equals x + 3, so the limit is 6.
cards.h: → quotient law needs lim g ≠ 0 → here lim g = 0 → 0/0 is not a value → rewrite first
cards.n: 'The limit does not exist because the denominator is 0' is wrong: the law's hypothesis fails, which says nothing about whether the limit exists.
o: Direct substitution gives 0/0, an indeterminate form, so no limit law yields the answer until the common factor is cancelled.
The quotient law is a theorem with a hypothesis; with lim(x − 3) = 0 the theorem simply does not apply.

w.a: The quotient law gives 0/0, which is 0.
w.why: 0/0 is indeterminate, not 0

w.a: The quotient law shows that the limit does not exist.
w.why: a failed hypothesis gives no conclusion at all

w.a: You cannot use the quotient law because the numerator is 0.
w.why: the hypothesis concerns the denominator's limit

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to 0} [f(x) + g(x)]$ can exist even when neither $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$ nor $\lim_{x \to 0} g(x)$ exists.
cards.a: The sum law says only: if both limits exist, the limit of the sum is their sum. It says nothing when they do not. Jumps can cancel: if f approaches 1 and 3 from the left and right while g approaches 2 and 0, the sum approaches 3 from both sides, so its limit is 3.
cards.h: → the law needs both limits → no conclusion otherwise → jumps can cancel → the sum's limit exists
cards.n: 'You can't add limits that don't exist, so the sum has no limit' reads the law backwards.
o: Take f(x) = |x|/x and g(x) = −|x|/x: neither has a limit at 0, but f + g = 0 for every x ≠ 0, so the sum's limit is 0.
Evaluate the sum one side at a time; if the one-sided sums agree, the sum's limit exists whatever f and g do separately.

w.a: The sum cannot have a limit, because the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits.
w.why: that law assumes both limits exist

w.a: The sum has a limit only if f and g are both continuous at 0.
w.why: continuity of f and g is not required

w.a: The limit of the sum is undefined plus undefined, which is undefined.
w.why: nonexistent limits cannot be added as numbers

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to 2} \sqrt{x^{2}+5}$ may be found by moving the limit inside the square root.
cards.a: For a composite, lim f(g(x)) = f(lim g(x)) when lim g(x) exists and f is continuous at that value. Here $\lim_{x \to 2} (x^{2}+5) = 9$ and √u is continuous at u = 9, so the limit is √9 = 3.
cards.h: → inner limit exists (9) → outer √ is continuous at 9 → the limit passes inside → 3
cards.n: 'You can always move limits inside functions' earns nothing; the outer function must be continuous at the inner limit.
o: √(x² + 5) is a composition of continuous functions, so it is continuous at x = 2 and its limit there equals its value √9 = 3.
The root law gives lim √(g(x)) = √(lim g(x)) whenever lim g(x) > 0.

w.a: You can move a limit inside any function.
w.why: this fails when the outer function is discontinuous there

w.a: The limit is 3 because √9 = 3.
w.why: states the arithmetic without the theorem or its hypothesis

cards.q: Describe the algebraic move for a limit of a rational expression that gives the form 0/0.
cards.a: Factor the numerator and the denominator; the 0/0 means both contain the factor (x − a). Cancel it, which is legal because x ≠ a throughout the limit, then substitute x = a into the simplified expression, which agrees with the original for every x ≠ a.
cards.h: → three steps, with why the middle one is legal
cards.n: Cancelling is legal only because x ≠ a in a limit; the original is still undefined at a, so never write f(a) = the simplified value.

cards.q: Describe the algebraic move for a 0/0 limit containing a square root.
cards.a: Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the radical expression (√A − B becomes √A + B), use (√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B² to clear the root, cancel the factor that produced the zero, then substitute.
cards.h: → one multiplication, one identity, then substitute
cards.n: Multiply the conjugate onto the top and the bottom, and leave the other side factored so the cancelling factor stays visible.

cards.q: Describe how to evaluate a 0/0 limit built from a complex (stacked) fraction.
cards.a: Combine the small fractions over a common denominator (or multiply the top and bottom of the big fraction by that common denominator), simplify until the factor that produced 0/0 appears in both numerator and denominator, cancel it, then substitute.
cards.n: Multiply every term of the top and the bottom by the same common denominator; clearing only the top changes the expression's value.

cards.q: State the special trigonometric limit involving sine of x over x.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$, with x in radians. More generally, if u → 0 then sin(u)/u → 1, so $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x}{3x} = 1$ and $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x}{x} = 3$. It is proved with the Squeeze Theorem, since cos x ≤ sin(x)/x ≤ 1 near 0.
cards.n: The argument of sine must match the denominator and go to 0: sin(3x)/x is not 1 but 3·sin(3x)/(3x) → 3.

cards.q: State the special trigonometric limit involving 1 minus cosine of x over x.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x} = 0$. Reason: multiplying by (1 + cos x)/(1 + cos x) gives $\frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot \frac{\sin x}{1+\cos x}$, which approaches 1·(0/2) = 0.
cards.n: Do not confuse it with $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}} = \frac{1}{2}$; the squared denominator changes the answer.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}$.
cards.n: The simplified x + 3 is continuous, but the original still has a hole at x = 3; writing '0/0 = 6' or 'f(3) = 6' loses credit.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x}$.
cards.a: 1/4. $\frac{\sqrt{x+4}-2}{x} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x+4}+2}{\sqrt{x+4}+2} = \frac{(x+4)-4}{x(\sqrt{x+4}+2)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x+4}+2}$ for x ≠ 0, which approaches $\frac{1}{2+2} = \frac{1}{4}$.
cards.n: Multiplying only the numerator by the conjugate changes the expression; multiply the top and the bottom.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{2+x}-\frac{1}{2}}{x}$.
cards.a: −1/4. $\frac{1}{2+x} - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2-(2+x)}{2(2+x)} = \frac{-x}{2(2+x)}$; dividing by x gives $\frac{-1}{2(2+x)}$ for x ≠ 0, which approaches $-\frac{1}{4}$.
cards.n: Dropping the minus sign in 2 − (2 + x) = −x gives +1/4; this limit is also the slope of 1/x at x = 2, as Unit 2 shows.

cards.q: Compute $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^{2} - 9}{x^{2} - x - 6}$.
cards.a: $\frac{6}{5}$. Factoring gives $\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{(x-3)(x+2)}$; for x ≠ 3 this equals $\frac{x+3}{x+2}$, which is $\frac{6}{5}$ at x = 3.
cards.n: The surviving factor x + 2 is nonzero at 3, so x = 3 is a hole (removable), not a vertical asymptote.

cards.q:
Evaluate each limit by rewriting in an equivalent form.
1. $\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{x^{2}-16}{x-4}$
2. $\lim_{x \to -3} \frac{x^{2}+5x+6}{x^{2}+3x}$
3. $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^{3}-8}{x-2}$
4. $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+2x-3}$
5. $\lim_{x \to -2} \frac{x+2}{x^{3}+8}$
6. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x+9}-3}{x}$
7. $\lim_{x \to 5} \frac{x-5}{\sqrt{x-1}-2}$
8. $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{\sqrt{x}-1}{x-1}$
9. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{x+4}-\frac{1}{4}}{x}$
10. $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(3+h)^{2}-9}{h}$
11. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 5x}{3x}$
12. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan x}{x}$
13. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 2x}{\sin 7x}$
14. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}}$
15. $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} \frac{x^{2}-4}{|x-2|}$
16. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^{2}+3x}{\sin x}$
cards.h: → 16 values, each with the rewrite that earns it
cards.n: Writing '= 0/0' and then a number, with no rewritten expression in between, earns nothing; the equivalent form is the work.

cards.q: Explain why cancelling the factor (x − 3) is legitimate when evaluating $\lim_{x \to 3} \frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}$.
cards.a: A limit as x → 3 uses only x ≠ 3, and for every such x, x − 3 ≠ 0, so (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x − 3) = x + 3 exactly. Functions that agree for all x near 3, except at 3, have the same limit there, so the limit is lim(x + 3) = 6.
cards.h: → the limit uses x ≠ 3 → x − 3 ≠ 0 there → the expressions agree near 3 → same limit
cards.n: 'Because the x − 3's cancel' names the move, not the reason; the reason is that x ≠ 3 throughout the limit.
o: The graphs of (x² − 9)/(x − 3) and x + 3 are identical except for the hole at (3, 6), and a limit ignores that single point.
Dividing by x − 3 is dividing by a nonzero number for every input that the limit examines.

w.a: You can cancel because x − 3 equals 0 at x = 3 anyway.
w.why: cancelling a zero factor is exactly what would be illegal

w.a: Cancelling shows that f(3) = 6.
w.why: f(3) stays undefined; only the limit is 6

w.a: You can always cancel common factors in any expression.
w.why: only where the factor is nonzero

cards.q: Explain why getting 0/0 from direct substitution does not mean the limit is 0, 1, or nonexistent.
cards.a: 0/0 is an indeterminate form: numerator and denominator both approach 0, but the form does not say how they compare, so the limit could be any number or fail to exist. (x² − 9)/(x − 3) → 6, while (x − 3)/(x − 3)² is unbounded near 3. An equivalent form must be found first.
cards.h: → both parts → 0 → their ratio is undetermined → any outcome is possible → rewrite first
cards.n: Writing '0/0, so the limit does not exist' or '0/0 = 1' earns nothing; 0/0 is a signal to rewrite, never a result.
o: x/x, 2x/x and x/x² all give 0/0 at x = 0, yet their limits are 1, 2 and nonexistent; the form alone cannot decide.
Factoring, conjugates or trig identities expose the common factor that makes both parts vanish; only after removing it can the limit be read.

w.a: 0/0 means the limit is 0 because the numerator is 0.
w.why: the denominator is also approaching 0

w.a: 0/0 means the limit does not exist because you cannot divide by 0.
w.why: many 0/0 limits exist

w.a: 0/0 equals 1 because anything divided by itself is 1.
w.why: 0/0 is indeterminate, not a number

cards.q: Explain why $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 3x}{x}$ equals 3 rather than 1.
cards.a: The special limit sin(u)/u → 1 needs the denominator to match the argument of sine. Rewrite $\frac{\sin 3x}{x} = 3 \cdot \frac{\sin 3x}{3x}$; with u = 3x → 0, sin(u)/u → 1, so the limit is 3·1 = 3.
cards.h: → argument 3x ≠ denominator x → multiply by 3/3 → sin u/u → 1 → the limit is 3
cards.n: Answering 1 because 'sine over x goes to 1' ignores that the argument and the denominator must match.
o: A table at x = 0.01 gives about 2.9996, supporting 3.
For small x, sin 3x ≈ 3x, so the quotient is approximately 3x/x = 3.

w.a: The limit is 1 because sin x over x always goes to 1.
w.why: the argument 3x does not match the denominator x

w.a: The limit is 1/3 because the 3 moves to the denominator.
w.why: the rewrite multiplies by 3; it does not divide

w.a: The limit does not exist because substitution gives 0/0.
w.why: 0/0 is indeterminate, not DNE

cards.q: Decide which technique to try first for $\lim_{x \to 5} \frac{x^{2}-25}{x-5}$, $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{4x-1}{2x+7}$, and $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 7x}{x}$.
cards.a: (1) Substitution gives 0/0 for a rational expression: factor and cancel, (x − 5)(x + 5)/(x − 5) = x + 5 → 10. (2) x → ∞ with polynomials: divide top and bottom by x (compare leading terms) → 4/2 = 2. (3) Substitution gives 0/0 with sine: match the special limit, 7·sin(7x)/(7x) → 7.
cards.n: Substituting and stopping at 0/0 or ∞/∞ earns nothing; the form only tells you which tool to use next.

cards.q: Describe a decision sequence for choosing a procedure to evaluate $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$.
cards.a: 1. Try direct substitution: if f is continuous at a, the value is the limit. 2. Nonzero/0: f is unbounded near a; check the sign on each side (±∞ or DNE). 3. 0/0: rewrite by factoring, a conjugate, combining fractions, or a trig identity with sin(u)/u. 4. Piecewise or |x − a|: one-sided limits. 5. Bounded factor times a factor → 0: Squeeze Theorem. 6. x → ±∞: compare highest powers.
cards.h: → ordered list of cases, one method each
cards.n: Stopping at 'nonzero/0 is undefined' misses the one-sided ±∞ analysis, and doing algebra before substituting wastes time.

cards.q: Identify the form that direct substitution gives in each limit, and what that form tells you to do next: (a) $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x+1}{x-2}$ (b) $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ (c) $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x-2}{x+1}$
cards.a: (a) 3/0, nonzero over zero: no algebra gives a finite limit; check the sides: left −∞, right +∞, so the limit does not exist (vertical asymptote x = 2). (b) 0/0, indeterminate: factor, (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 → 4. (c) 0/3, an actual value: the limit is 0, with no further work.
cards.h: → form, meaning, next step, for each
cards.n: Treating 0/3 like 0/0 (more algebra), or 3/0 like 0/0 (trying to factor), is the classification error this topic targets.

cards.q:
Determine each limit (value, ±∞, or DNE) and name the procedure used.
1. $\lim_{x \to 2} (x^{3}-2x+1)$
2. $\lim_{x \to -1} \frac{x^{2}-1}{x+1}$
3. $\lim_{x \to 9} \frac{\sqrt{x}-3}{x-9}$
4. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 4x}{x}$
5. $\lim_{x \to 0} x\cos\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$
6. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{5x^{3}-x}{2x^{3}+7}$
7. $\lim_{x \to 3^{+}} \frac{x+1}{x-3}$
8. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\frac{1}{3+x}-\frac{1}{3}}{x}$
9. $\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{|x-4|}{x-4}$
10. $\lim_{x \to \pi} \frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$
11. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1-\cos x}{\sin x}$
12. $\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{3x+1}{\sqrt{x^{2}+4}}$
13. $\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(1+h)^{2}-1}{h}$
14. $\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^{3}-1}{x^{2}-1}$
15. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^{2}+1}{x-3}$
16. $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\tan 3x}{2x}$
17. $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$, f(x) = x² for x < 2, 3x − 2 for x ≥ 2
18. $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\cos x}{x}$
cards.a:
1 → substitution (polynomial): 5
2 → factor, (x − 1)(x + 1)/(x + 1): −2
3 → conjugate (or x − 9 = (√x − 3)(√x + 3)): 1/6
4 → special trig limit, 4·sin(4x)/(4x): 4
5 → Squeeze, −|x| ≤ x cos(1/x) ≤ |x|: 0
6 → divide by x³ (leading terms): 5/2
7 → sign of 4/(small positive): +∞, unbounded
8 → combine fractions, −1/(3(3 + x)): −1/9
9 → one-sided limits −1 and 1: DNE
10 → substitution (continuous at π): −1
11 → trig rewrite, [(1 − cos x)/x]·[x/sin x] → 0·1: 0
12 → divide by |x| = −x for x < 0: −3
13 → expand, (2h + h²)/h: 2
14 → factor, (x² + x + 1)/(x + 1): 3/2
15 → degree of top exceeds bottom: ∞, unbounded
16 → trig rewrite, (3/2)·[sin 3x/(3x)]·[1/cos 3x]: 3/2
17 → one-sided limits, 4 and 4: 4
18 → Squeeze, ±1/x for x > 0: 0
cards.h: → one line each: procedure, then value
cards.n: 'Substitution gives 0/0' is not a procedure; each 0/0 item needs a named rewrite, and item 7 needs a sign check, not algebra.

cards.q: Decide on two different valid procedures for $\lim_{x \to 4} \frac{x-4}{\sqrt{x}-2}$, and carry out one.
cards.a: Procedure 1: factor x − 4 as a difference of squares, (√x − 2)(√x + 2), and cancel √x − 2. Procedure 2: multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √x + 2, giving (x − 4)(√x + 2)/(x − 4). Either way, for x ≠ 4 the expression equals √x + 2, so the limit is √4 + 2 = 4.
cards.h: → two methods named, one worked, the value
cards.n: Squaring the numerator and denominator to 'remove the root' changes the value; only multiplying by a form of 1 is allowed.

cards.q: Decide which procedure is required for $\lim_{x \to 0} g(x)$ when g(x) = cos x for x < 0 and g(x) = x + 1 for x ≥ 0, and determine the limit.
cards.a: One-sided limits, because x = 0 is where the formula changes. Left: $\lim_{x \to 0^{-}} \cos x = 1$. Right: $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} (x+1) = 1$. Both equal 1, so $\lim_{x \to 0} g(x) = 1$.
cards.h: → procedure named, two one-sided limits, verdict
cards.n: Substituting 0 into the x ≥ 0 piece alone gives only the right-hand limit; the conclusion needs both sides stated.

cards.q: Decide which procedure applies to $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \sqrt{x}\,\cos\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$, explain why the product law fails, and evaluate the limit.
cards.a: The Squeeze Theorem. The product law fails because $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \cos(1/x)$ does not exist (it oscillates). Since −1 ≤ cos(1/x) ≤ 1 and √x ≥ 0, $-\sqrt{x} \le \sqrt{x}\cos(1/x) \le \sqrt{x}$ for x > 0; both bounds approach 0 as x → 0⁺, so the limit is 0.
cards.h: → procedure, why the product law fails, the squeeze
cards.n: Writing lim √x · lim cos(1/x) = 0 · (something) = 0 earns nothing: the second limit does not exist, so the product law cannot be used.

cards.q: Explain why direct substitution should be the first procedure tried when evaluating a limit.
cards.a: If the function is continuous at the point, as polynomial, rational, root, trig, exponential and log functions are on their domains, the limit equals the function value and substitution finishes the problem. If it fails, the form it produces (0/0, nonzero/0) tells which procedure comes next.
cards.h: → continuous → limit = value → done; otherwise the form it gives classifies the next step
cards.n: 'Because it is easiest' misses the justification: substitution is valid exactly when the function is continuous at the point.
o: Substitution both answers the continuous cases and diagnoses the rest: 0/0 calls for rewriting, nonzero/0 for a sign analysis.
The standard function families are continuous on their domains, so for an input in the domain the limit is f(a) at once.

w.a: You substitute first because the limit always equals f(a).
w.why: only when f is continuous at a

w.a: Substitution comes first because it is the only method that gives exact answers.
w.why: factoring and squeezing give exact answers too

w.a: If substitution gives 0/0, the limit does not exist, so you can stop.
w.why: 0/0 is indeterminate; rewrite and continue

cards.q: Explain why no amount of factoring will produce a finite value for $\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{x+1}{x-2}$.
cards.a: Substitution gives 3/0: the numerator approaches 3, not 0, so there is no common factor (x − 2) to cancel. A quantity near 3 divided by values approaching 0 grows without bound, so the function is unbounded near 2 (left −∞, right +∞) and the limit does not exist.
cards.h: → numerator → 3 ≠ 0 → no common factor → nonzero over tiny → unbounded → DNE
cards.n: 'It's undefined at 2, so factor and cancel' misclassifies nonzero/0 as 0/0; only 0/0 signals a factor that can cancel.
o: x − 2 is a factor of the denominator but not of the numerator (x + 1 is 3 at x = 2), so x = 2 is a vertical asymptote, not a hole.
A sign check shows the quotient is negative just left of 2 and positive just right, with magnitude growing without bound on both sides.

w.a: Factoring will work; you just need to find the right factorization.
w.why: the numerator has no factor of x − 2

w.a: The limit is 0 because the denominator is 0.
w.why: dividing by values near 0 makes the quotient large, not zero

w.a: The limit is 3 because the numerator approaches 3.
w.why: ignores the denominator's approach to 0

cards.q: State the Squeeze Theorem, including its hypotheses.
cards.a: If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) for all x in an open interval containing a (except possibly at a itself), and $\lim_{x \to a} g(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L$, then $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$. The same holds for one-sided limits, and for x → ±∞, when the inequality holds on the matching interval.
cards.n: The two outer limits must be EQUAL and the inequality must hold near a, not just at a; bounds such as −1 ≤ f(x) ≤ 1 give no conclusion.

cards.q: Describe how to set up a squeeze for a function like f(x) = x² sin(1/x) near x = 0.
cards.a: Start from −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1, true for all x ≠ 0. Multiply through by x², which is nonnegative, so the inequalities keep their direction: −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x². Since $\lim_{x \to 0} (-x^{2}) = 0 = \lim_{x \to 0} x^{2}$, the Squeeze Theorem gives $\lim_{x \to 0} x^{2}\sin(1/x) = 0$.
cards.h: → a starting inequality, one multiplication, two limits
cards.n: Multiplying an inequality by a quantity that can be negative reverses it; state why the multiplier is nonnegative (x² ≥ 0).

cards.q: Use the Squeeze Theorem to evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} x^{4}\cos\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$.
cards.a: 0. For x ≠ 0, −1 ≤ cos(1/x) ≤ 1, and multiplying by x⁴ ≥ 0 gives −x⁴ ≤ x⁴cos(1/x) ≤ x⁴. Both bounds approach 0 as x → 0, so by the Squeeze Theorem the limit is 0.
cards.n: Direct substitution fails because cos(1/x) has no limit at 0; writing 0·cos(1/0) = 0 earns nothing.

cards.q: Given that $2x \le g(x) \le x^{2} + 1$ for all x near 1, apply the Squeeze Theorem to find $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x)$.
cards.a: 2. The inequality holds for all x near 1. Both bounds are polynomials, so $\lim_{x \to 1} 2x = 2$ and $\lim_{x \to 1} (x^{2}+1) = 2$. The outer limits are equal, so by the Squeeze Theorem $\lim_{x \to 1} g(x) = 2$.
cards.n: The scored step is stating that the two outer limits are equal before concluding; g(1) itself is never needed and may not even equal 2.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} x\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$, giving the bounding functions.
cards.a: 0. For x ≠ 0, |x sin(1/x)| = |x|·|sin(1/x)| ≤ |x|, so −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|. Both $\lim_{x \to 0} (-|x|)$ and $\lim_{x \to 0} |x|$ equal 0, so by the Squeeze Theorem the limit is 0.
cards.n: The bounds −x ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ x are false for x < 0, since multiplying by a negative x reverses the inequalities; use |x|.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\sin x}{x}$ using the Squeeze Theorem.
cards.a: 0. For x > 0, −1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1, and dividing by x > 0 keeps the direction: $-\frac{1}{x} \le \frac{\sin x}{x} \le \frac{1}{x}$. Both bounds approach 0 as x → ∞, so the limit is 0. The graph crosses its horizontal asymptote y = 0 infinitely often.
cards.h: → bound sin x, divide by x > 0, squeeze
cards.n: Confusing this with $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ is the trap: where x is heading decides which tool applies.

cards.q: Find $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)$, given that 4x − 9 ≤ f(x) ≤ x² − 4x + 7 for x ≥ 0, and verify the hypotheses of the theorem you use.
cards.a: 7, by the Squeeze Theorem. The inequality holds on an open interval containing 4 (for example (3, 5), inside x ≥ 0). $\lim_{x \to 4} (4x - 9) = 7$ and $\lim_{x \to 4} (x^{2} - 4x + 7) = 16 - 16 + 7 = 7$. The outer limits are equal, so $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = 7$.
cards.h: → theorem, interval, two outer limits, conclusion
cards.n: Omitting that the inequality holds on an open interval containing 4, or that the two outer limits are equal, drops the justification point.

cards.q: Determine what can be concluded about $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$ if 1 − x² ≤ f(x) ≤ 3 + x² for all x.
cards.a: Nothing about its value, and not even that it exists. The lower bound approaches 1 and the upper bound approaches 3; since 1 ≠ 3, the Squeeze Theorem does not apply. We learn only that f stays between values near 1 and 3; f could approach 2, or oscillate between them with no limit.
cards.h: → compare the two outer limits, then the (non)conclusion
cards.n: Concluding the limit is 2, the average of the bounds, is the classic misuse; equal outer limits are a hypothesis, not a suggestion.

cards.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} \sqrt{x}\, e^{\sin(\pi/x)}$.
cards.a: 0. Since −1 ≤ sin(π/x) ≤ 1 and e^u is increasing, $e^{-1} \le e^{\sin(\pi/x)} \le e$. Multiplying by √x ≥ 0 gives $\frac{\sqrt{x}}{e} \le \sqrt{x}\,e^{\sin(\pi/x)} \le e\sqrt{x}$ for x > 0. Both bounds approach 0 as x → 0⁺, so by the Squeeze Theorem the limit is 0.
cards.h: → bound the sine, exponentiate, multiply by √x, squeeze
cards.n: The limit is one-sided because √x needs x > 0; the Squeeze Theorem works for a one-sided limit when the inequality holds on an interval (0, c).

cards.q: Identify the inequality and the theorem used to show $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.
cards.a: For 0 < |x| < π/2, cos x ≤ sin(x)/x ≤ 1, an inequality that comes from comparing areas of two triangles and a sector of the unit circle. Since $\lim_{x \to 0} \cos x = 1$ and the upper bound is the constant 1, the Squeeze Theorem gives $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$.
cards.h: → the double inequality, the two outer limits, the theorem
cards.n: The area argument behind the inequality is background; the exam uses the result sin(x)/x → 1 and expects the squeeze structure to be recognized.

cards.q: Explain why the product law cannot be used to evaluate $\lim_{x \to 0} x^{2}\sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$, and what replaces it.
cards.a: The product law needs both factor limits to exist, but $\lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x)$ does not exist (it oscillates). The Squeeze Theorem replaces it: −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x², both bounds → 0, so the limit is 0.
cards.h: → the product law needs both limits → sin(1/x) has none → squeeze with ±x² → 0
cards.n: '0 times anything is 0' earns nothing; there is no number to multiply by, which is exactly why the squeeze is needed.
o: Since |x² sin(1/x)| ≤ x² → 0, the values are forced to 0 whatever the oscillation does; that bound is the squeeze in absolute-value form.
A bounded factor times a factor approaching 0 approaches 0, and the Squeeze Theorem is what justifies that fact.

w.a: The limit is 0 because lim x² = 0 and 0 times anything is 0.
w.why: the other factor has no limit to multiply

w.a: The limit does not exist because sin(1/x) does not exist at 0.
w.why: a product can have a limit when one factor has none

w.a: The product law gives 0·sin(1/0) = 0.
w.why: sin(1/0) is undefined

cards.q: Explain why −x ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ x is not a valid squeeze for all x near 0, and give a valid one.
cards.a: Multiplying −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 by x keeps the direction only for x > 0; for x < 0 it reverses, giving x ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ −x, so the stated inequality fails there. Valid: −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x| for all x ≠ 0, with both bounds → 0.
cards.h: → multiplying by a negative x reverses → the inequality fails for x < 0 → use ±|x|
cards.n: Using ±x unchanged on both sides of 0 is the error graders flag; either use |x| or treat each side separately.
o: Treat the sides separately: for x > 0 use −x ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ x; for x < 0 use x ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ −x; each pair of bounds → 0.
|x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x| holds for all x ≠ 0 and gives the squeeze directly.

w.a: It is valid because x is small near 0.
w.why: being small does not fix the sign problem

w.a: The bounds are fine since both −x and x go to 0.
w.why: equal limits do not help if the inequality is false for x < 0

w.a: You only need the inequality for positive x.
w.why: a two-sided limit needs it on both sides

cards.q: Explain why knowing 1 ≤ f(x) ≤ 3 near x = 0 does not determine $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$.
cards.a: The Squeeze Theorem needs the lower and upper bounds to approach the same number. Here they approach 1 and 3, which differ, so the hypothesis fails. f could approach any value in [1, 3], or oscillate between 1 and 3 with no limit at all.
cards.h: → outer limits 1 and 3 → unequal → hypothesis fails → no conclusion
cards.n: 'The limit is between 1 and 3' is not a limit, and '2' is a guess; unequal bounds give no conclusion.
o: Counterexamples: f(x) = 2 has limit 2, while f(x) = 2 + sin(1/x) stays between 1 and 3 but has no limit at 0.
Bounds that do not pinch together leave room for f to move, so they cannot force a single value.

w.a: The limit is 2 because it is the midpoint of the bounds.
w.why: unequal bounds force no value

w.a: The limit exists because f is bounded.
w.why: bounded functions can oscillate without a limit

w.a: The limit is 1 because f is always at least 1.
w.why: a lower bound is not a limit

cards.a: About 3. From the left, 2.85 and 2.985 increase toward 3; from the right, 3.15 and 3.015 decrease toward 3. The data match the line y = 1.5x, so graphically the curve heads to the point (2, 3), and in notation the estimate is $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 3$.
cards.h: → one value, with both one-sided trends
cards.n: A table supports only an estimate, and it says nothing about f(2); writing 'f(2) = 3' makes a different, unsupported claim.

cards.q: Contrast what a table of values and an algebraic simplification can each establish about $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$.
cards.a: A table gives numerical evidence: it suggests the value the limit appears to have, a conjecture that sampling can mislead (sin(π/x) is 0 at every x = 1/n, yet has no limit at 0). Algebra, such as factoring or rationalizing to an expression continuous at a, establishes the exact value with certainty, because it covers every x near a.
cards.n: Presenting a table as proof, or giving an algebraic answer with no rewritten expression shown, loses the justification; say 'appears to' for a table.

cards.q:
Translate each description into limit notation.
1. As x approaches 4, f(x) approaches −2.
2. As x approaches 1 from the left, g(x) approaches 6.
3. h(x) increases without bound as x approaches 0 from the right.
4. As x decreases without bound, p(x) approaches 3.
5. q(t) can be made as close to 10 as we like by taking t close enough to 2, t ≠ 2.
6. f(x) decreases without bound as x approaches −3 from either side.
7. As x increases without bound, r(x) increases without bound.
8. The graph of k has the horizontal asymptote y = 1 on the right.
9. The graph of m has a hole at (5, 2) and no point on x = 5.
10. The graph of w has the vertical asymptote x = 7 and rises without bound just right of it.
cards.a:
1 → $\lim_{x \to 4} f(x) = -2$
2 → $\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} g(x) = 6$
3 → $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} h(x) = \infty$
4 → $\lim_{x \to -\infty} p(x) = 3$
5 → $\lim_{t \to 2} q(t) = 10$
6 → $\lim_{x \to -3} f(x) = -\infty$
7 → $\lim_{x \to \infty} r(x) = \infty$
8 → $\lim_{x \to \infty} k(x) = 1$
9 → $\lim_{x \to 5} m(x) = 2$, with m(5) undefined
10 → $\lim_{x \to 7^{+}} w(x) = \infty$
cards.n: Writing x → ∞ for 'decreases without bound' (item 4), or dropping the side in items 2, 3 and 10, changes the statement.

cards.q: Represent, in words precise enough to draw, a graph of a function f on [−1, 4] with $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = -1$ and f(0) undefined, $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} f(x) = 1$, $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} f(x) = 3$, f(2) = 3, and f continuous at every other point of [−1, 4].
cards.a: One graph that works: the line y = x − 1 from the filled point (−1, −2) to an open circle at (2, 1), with an open circle at (0, −1) and no point above or below it; then a filled point at (2, 3) and the horizontal segment y = 3 from (2, 3) to the filled point (4, 3). The hole gives limit −1 with f(0) undefined; at x = 2 the left piece ends at height 1 and the right piece starts at the filled height 3.
cards.h: → the figure in words: pieces, open and filled points
cards.n: Filling the dot at (2, 1) instead of (2, 3) contradicts f(2) = 3, and any point on x = 0 contradicts 'f(0) undefined'.

cards.q: Represent the statements $\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} f(x) = 2$ and $\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} f(x) = 5$ with a table of six values of f, three on each side of x = 1.
cards.a:
x · f(x)
0.9 · 1.9
0.99 · 1.99
0.999 · 1.999
1.001 · 5.001
1.01 · 5.01
1.1 · 5.1
The left values close in on 2 and the right values on 5, so the two-sided limit appears not to exist (a jump at x = 1). Any values with these two trends are correct.
cards.h: → six-row table, then what it shows
cards.n: A table whose right-side values also approach 2 represents a different function; each side must head to its own one-sided limit.

cards.q: Describe the graph of f(x) = (x² − x − 2)/(x − 2) near x = 2, give three table values on each side of x = 2, and state $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$.
cards.h: → simplified formula, graph in words, table, limit
cards.n: Drawing the full line with no hole, or listing f(2) = 3 in the table, misrepresents f: 2 is not in its domain.

cards.q: Determine $\lim_{x \to 1} f(g(x))$ from these data: a table of g gives g(0.9) = 2.9, g(0.99) = 2.99, g(1.01) = 2.99, g(1.1) = 2.9; near x = 3 the graph of f is the line y = x + 1 on both sides, with an open circle at (3, 4) and a filled point at (3, 1).
cards.a: 4. The table suggests g(x) → 3 as x → 1, with g(x) < 3 on both sides, so the inputs to f approach 3 from the left. On the graph, $\lim_{u \to 3} f(u) = 4$ (the line heads to the open circle), so $\lim_{x \to 1} f(g(x)) = 4$. The filled point f(3) = 1 is not used, since the inputs g(x) stay below 3.
cards.h: → inner limit from the table, then f's limit from the graph
cards.n: Answering f(3) = 1 uses the filled point, which would matter only if g(x) equalled 3 near x = 1; the table suggests it stays below 3.

cards.q: Determine $\lim_{t \to 0^{+}} f\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)$, given $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = 3$, and explain the re-expression.
cards.a: 3. Let x = 1/t. As t → 0⁺, x = 1/t increases without bound, so f(1/t) = f(x) with x → ∞, and the values approach 3. Graphically, the behavior of f far to the right (its horizontal asymptote y = 3) becomes the behavior of f(1/t) just to the right of t = 0.
cards.h: → substitute x = 1/t, then track where x goes
cards.n: Letting t → 0⁻ instead sends 1/t → −∞, which needs the limit of f at −∞, not given here; the side of approach matters.

cards.q: Explain how a graph with an open circle at (2, 3) and a filled dot at (2, 5) can show both $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 3$ and f(2) = 5.
cards.a: The open circle marks the height the curve approaches from both sides, so both one-sided limits are 3 and the limit is 3. The filled dot marks the actual function value, f(2) = 5. Limits describe nearby values and function values describe the point, so the two statements are consistent.
cards.h: → open circle = height approached → filled dot = value → a limit uses nearby x → both hold
cards.n: 'The graph contradicts itself' earns nothing; this is the standard picture of a removable discontinuity.
o: In notation the graph says $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 3 \ne 5 = f(2)$, so f has a removable discontinuity at x = 2.
A table for this f would show values near 3 for x near 2 and the entry 5 at x = 2 itself.

w.a: The limit is 5 because the filled dot is the real point.
w.why: the filled dot gives the value, not the limit

w.a: The limit does not exist because there are two points at x = 2.
w.why: only one point is filled; the other is a hole

w.a: f(2) is 3 because the curve goes there.
w.why: the open circle means the curve omits that point

cards.q: Explain why the graphs of $y = \frac{x^{2}-4}{x-2}$ and y = x + 2 give the same limit at every point, yet represent different functions.
cards.a: For every x ≠ 2 the two formulas give equal values, and a limit depends only on values near the point, excluding the point. So every limit matches, including 4 at x = 2. They differ only at x = 2: the first is undefined there (a hole at (2, 4)); the second equals 4.
cards.h: → equal for x ≠ 2 → limits ignore single points → same limits → differ only at x = 2
cards.n: 'They are the same function because one simplifies to the other' ignores the domain; simplifying does not add x = 2 to it.
o: The first function has a removable discontinuity at x = 2 and the second is continuous there; the discontinuity does not change any limit.
Tables of the two agree in every row except x = 2, where the first gives an error and the second gives 4.

w.a: They are the same function since the x − 2 cancels.
w.why: their domains differ at x = 2

w.a: They have different limits at x = 2 because one is undefined there.
w.why: being undefined at a point does not change the limit

w.a: The graphs look identical, so the functions are identical.
w.why: a graph can hide a one-point hole

cards.q: Contrast removable, jump, and infinite discontinuity.
cards.a: Removable: $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists (finite) but f(a) is undefined or unequal to it: a hole. Jump: both one-sided limits exist (finite) but differ: the graph breaks to a new height. Infinite: at least one one-sided limit is +∞ or −∞: a vertical asymptote at x = a. Only the removable kind has a two-sided limit.
cards.h: → three types: the limit condition and the picture for each
cards.n: Only the removable kind can be repaired by redefining one value; calling a jump 'removable' because both sides have limits is the classic mislabel.

cards.q: A function f satisfies $\lim_{x \to 5} f(x) = 7$ but f(5) = 2. Identify the type of discontinuity at x = 5.
cards.a: Removable. The two-sided limit exists and is finite (7), but it does not equal f(5) = 2, so the third continuity condition fails; redefining f(5) = 7 would make f continuous at x = 5.
cards.h: → type, then the limit fact that decides it
cards.n: 'Removable' refers to the limit existing, not to the size of the gap between 7 and 2; 'removable' without the value 7 is incomplete.

cards.q: Identify what the graph of f looks like at a removable discontinuity.
cards.a: An open circle at (a, L), where L is the common value of the two one-sided limits, with the curve approaching that height from both sides. If f(a) is defined, a separate filled dot sits at (a, f(a)) above or below the hole; if not, there is no point on the line x = a.
cards.n: A hole is still a discontinuity even with no filled dot anywhere on x = a; f(a) is then simply undefined.

cards.q:
Classify the discontinuity of each function at the given x-value as removable, jump, or infinite (vertical asymptote), or say it is none of these.
1. (x² − 4)/(x − 2) at x = 2
2. 1/(x − 5) at x = 5
3. |x|/x at x = 0
4. (x + 1)/(x² − 1) at x = −1
5. (x + 1)/(x² − 1) at x = 1
6. ⌊x⌋ (greatest integer) at x = 2
7. sin(x)/x at x = 0
8. tan x at x = π/2
9. x² for x < 1 and x + 3 for x ≥ 1, at x = 1
10. 1/x² at x = 0
11. x² − 1 for x ≠ 3, with f(3) = 0, at x = 3
12. ln|x| at x = 0
13. $2^{1/x}$ at x = 0
14. sin(1/x) at x = 0
cards.a:
1 → removable: limit 4, f(2) undefined
2 → infinite: −∞ from the left, +∞ from the right
3 → jump: −1 from the left, 1 from the right
4 → removable: 1/(x − 1) for x ≠ −1, limit −1/2
5 → infinite: 1/(x − 1) is unbounded at 1
6 → jump: left-hand limit 1, right-hand limit 2
7 → removable: limit 1, f(0) undefined
8 → infinite: +∞ from the left, −∞ from the right
9 → jump: left-hand limit 1, right-hand limit 4
10 → infinite: +∞ from both sides, no finite limit
11 → removable: limit 8 ≠ f(3) = 0
12 → infinite: −∞ from both sides
13 → infinite: +∞ from the right (from the left it → 0)
14 → none of the three: oscillation, and neither one-sided limit exists
cards.h: → type + the limit evidence, one per line
cards.n: Item 10 is the trap: both sides agree at +∞, but no finite limit exists, so it is infinite, not removable; item 14 fits none of the three types.

cards.q: Identify each discontinuity of f and its type, where the graph of f on [0, 8] is a curve with an open circle at (2, 4) and a filled point at (2, 1); at x = 5 the curve approaches height 3 from the left, and a filled point at (5, 6) starts the curve on the right; x = 7 is a vertical asymptote, with the curve falling without bound from both sides.
cards.a: x = 2: removable (the limit is 4 but f(2) = 1). x = 5: jump (left-hand limit 3, right-hand limit 6). x = 7: infinite, a vertical asymptote, with $\lim_{x \to 7} f(x) = -\infty$ and f(7) undefined. f is continuous at every other point of (0, 8).
cards.h: → each x-value: type and the evidence
cards.n: Calling x = 5 removable because f(5) is defined misreads the definition; the one-sided limits differ, which makes it a jump.

cards.q: Determine the x-values where $f(x) = \frac{x^{2}-x-6}{x^{2}-9}$ is discontinuous, and classify each discontinuity.
cards.a: x = 3: removable. f(x) = (x − 3)(x + 2)/((x − 3)(x + 3)) = (x + 2)/(x + 3) for x ≠ 3, so the limit at 3 is 5/6 while f(3) is undefined. x = −3: infinite. The factor x + 3 does not cancel, and the simplified numerator x + 2 is −1 ≠ 0 there, so f is unbounded near −3: vertical asymptote x = −3.
cards.h: → factor, cancel, test each zero of the denominator
cards.n: Calling both zeros of x² − 9 vertical asymptotes skips the numerator check; the cancelled factor (x − 3) gives a hole.

cards.q: Determine the type of discontinuity at x = 2 of f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2, f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2, with the limits that show it.
cards.a: A jump discontinuity. $\lim_{x \to 2^{-}} (x+1) = 3$ and $\lim_{x \to 2^{+}} x^{2} = 4$; both one-sided limits exist but 3 ≠ 4, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist, even though f(2) = 4 is defined.
cards.h: → both one-sided limits, then the type
cards.n: f(2) = 4 matching the right-hand limit does not make f continuous; agreement with one side is not enough at an interior point.

cards.q: Identify the type of discontinuity at x = −1 of a function g with $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} g(x) = -\infty$, $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} g(x) = 2$, and g(−1) = 2.
cards.a: An infinite discontinuity: x = −1 is a vertical asymptote. One unbounded one-sided limit is enough; the finite right-hand limit and g(−1) = 2 do not change that. It is not a jump, because a jump needs both one-sided limits to be finite.
cards.h: → type, then which limit decides it
cards.n: Calling it a jump, or 'continuous from the right, so fine', misses that one unbounded side makes x = −1 a vertical asymptote.

cards.q: Explain why the discontinuity of $\frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}$ at x = 3 is removable rather than a vertical asymptote.
cards.a: The numerator is also 0 at x = 3: x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so for x ≠ 3 the function equals x + 3, and its limit at 3 is 6, a finite number. A finite two-sided limit with f(3) undefined is a removable discontinuity (a hole at (3, 6)), not a vertical asymptote.
cards.h: → numerator also 0 → the common factor cancels → finite limit 6 → a hole, not an asymptote
cards.n: 'The denominator is zero at 3, so there is an asymptote' earns nothing; the numerator must be checked before claiming one.
o: A vertical asymptote needs an infinite one-sided limit; here both one-sided limits equal 6, so there is none.
A table near 3 shows values near 6 (5.9, 5.99, 6.01, 6.1), not values growing without bound.

w.a: It is a vertical asymptote because the denominator is zero at x = 3.
w.why: the numerator is zero too, so the factor cancels

w.a: It is removable because f(3) = 6 after cancelling.
w.why: f(3) is undefined; the limit is 6

w.a: It is a jump because the function is undefined at 3.
w.why: a jump needs unequal one-sided limits

cards.q: Explain why $f(x) = \frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}$ has a discontinuity at x = 2 that is not removable, even though both one-sided limits are +∞.
cards.a: A removable discontinuity needs the two-sided limit to exist as a finite number, so that f(2) could be defined to equal it. Here f grows without bound on both sides; ∞ is not a real number, so no value of f(2) can match it. It is an infinite discontinuity: x = 2 is a vertical asymptote.
cards.h: → removable needs a finite limit → both sides unbounded → no value can fill it → infinite discontinuity
cards.n: 'Both sides agree, so it is removable' treats ∞ as a number; agreement at ∞ is still unboundedness.
o: Writing lim = ∞ describes how the limit fails to exist, and removability requires a limit that exists.
Whatever value is assigned to f(2), f stays unbounded near 2, so continuity cannot be achieved.

w.a: It is removable because the left and right limits are equal.
w.why: equal infinite behaviors are not a finite limit

w.a: It is removable by defining f(2) = ∞.
w.why: ∞ is not a function value

w.a: It is a jump discontinuity because f jumps up to infinity.
w.why: a jump needs finite, unequal one-sided limits

cards.q: Explain why a function with $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} g(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} g(x) = 2$ has an infinite discontinuity at x = −1 rather than a jump.
cards.a: A jump needs both one-sided limits to exist as finite numbers that differ. Here the left-hand behavior is unbounded (−∞), and one unbounded side is enough to make x = −1 a vertical asymptote, so the discontinuity is infinite.
cards.h: → a jump needs two finite one-sided limits → the left side is unbounded → vertical asymptote
cards.n: 'It jumps from −∞ to 2' misuses the word; the classification rests on whether each one-sided limit is finite.
o: The line x = −1 is a vertical asymptote because at least one one-sided limit is infinite, which is what an infinite discontinuity is.
Only finite one-sided limits can be compared as a jump; −∞ is not a height the graph jumps from.

w.a: It is a jump because the two sides do not match.
w.why: a jump requires both sides finite

w.a: It is removable because the right-hand limit equals g(−1).
w.why: the two-sided limit does not exist

w.a: It is continuous from the right, so there is no real discontinuity.
w.why: continuity at −1 needs the two-sided limit

cards.q: State the three conditions required for f to be continuous at x = a.
cards.a: (1) f(a) is defined. (2) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists. (3) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$. All three must hold; if any one fails, f is discontinuous at x = a.
cards.n: On free response a continuity justification must address all three explicitly, including that the limit exists (both one-sided limits agree).

cards.q: f approaches 3 as x→2 from the left but -1 from the right, with f(2)=3. Identify $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$, and state whether f is continuous at x=2.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ does not exist, because the one-sided limits disagree (3 versus −1). So f is not continuous at x = 2: the second condition fails, whatever f(2) is. The value f(2) = 3 matches only the left side, which makes f continuous from the left at 2, not continuous there.
cards.h: → one-sided comparison, then the continuity verdict
cards.n: A defined f(2) that matches one side gives only one-sided continuity; continuity at x = 2 needs the two-sided limit to exist.

cards.q: Write the definition of continuity of f at x = c as a single equation, and explain why that equation contains all three conditions.
cards.a: $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$. Writing it asserts that the right side, f(c), exists (condition 1), that the left side, the limit, exists as a number (condition 2), and that the two are equal (condition 3).
cards.h: → one equation, then what it asserts
cards.n: Writing this equation for a specific function without showing the limit exists (both one-sided limits agree) assumes what needs proving.

cards.q: Justify whether f is continuous at x = 2, where f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 4.
cards.a: f is continuous at x = 2. (1) f(2) = 4 is defined. (2) For x ≠ 2, f(x) = x + 2, so $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 4$ exists. (3) $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 4 = f(2)$. All three conditions hold.
cards.n: 'Yes, because f(2) = 4' names one condition; the limit must be computed and compared with f(2).

cards.q: Justify whether f is continuous at x = 2, where f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2 and f(2) = 5, naming any condition that fails.
cards.a: f is not continuous at x = 2. f(2) = 5 is defined and $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 2} (x+2) = 4$ exists, but 4 ≠ 5, so the third condition, $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = f(2)$, fails. The discontinuity is removable.
cards.h: → verdict, then the condition that fails
cards.n: 'Not continuous because of 0/0' earns nothing: the formula for x ≠ 2 is never evaluated at 2, and the failure is limit ≠ value.

cards.q: Justify that f is continuous at x = 1, where f(x) = 2x + 3 for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = x² + 4 for x > 1.
cards.a: f(1) = 2(1) + 3 = 5. $\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} (2x+3) = 5$ and $\lim_{x \to 1^{+}} (x^{2}+4) = 5$, so $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 5$ exists. Since $\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 5 = f(1)$, f is continuous at x = 1.
cards.n: Showing only that the two formulas agree at x = 1 skips the explicit statements that the limit exists and equals f(1), which earn the point.

cards.q:
Identify the first of the three continuity conditions at x = 2 that fails in each case, or write 'continuous'.
1. f(2) undefined; $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$
2. f(2) = 5; left-hand limit 5, right-hand limit 1
3. f(2) = 3; $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$
4. f(2) = 5; $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x) = 5$
5. f(x) = 1/(x − 2)
6. f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2, f(2) = 4
7. f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2, 2x − 1 for x ≥ 2
8. f(x) = x for x ≤ 2, x² for x > 2
9. f(x) = |x − 2|
10. f(x) = ⌊x⌋ (greatest integer)
cards.a:
1 → condition 1 (f(2) undefined): removable
2 → condition 2 (one-sided limits differ): jump
3 → condition 3 (5 ≠ 3): removable
4 → continuous
5 → condition 1 (f(2) undefined; the limit fails too): infinite
6 → continuous (limit 4 = f(2))
7 → continuous (left 3, right 3, f(2) = 3)
8 → condition 2 (left 2, right 4): jump
9 → continuous (limit 0 = f(2))
10 → condition 2 (left 1, right 2): jump
cards.n: Stopping at 'discontinuous' without naming the failed condition is what loses the justification point on free response.

cards.q: Justify whether f is continuous at x = 0, where f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0.
cards.a: f is continuous at x = 0. f(0) = 0 is defined. Since −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x| for x ≠ 0 and both bounds approach 0, the Squeeze Theorem gives $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0$. So $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0 = f(0)$.
cards.h: → f(0), the limit by squeeze, equality
cards.n: 'sin(1/x) is undefined at 0, so f is discontinuous' ignores that f(0) is defined separately and that the limit comes from squeezing.

cards.q: Explain why f(c) being defined and $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ existing are not enough to make f continuous at c.
cards.a: Continuity also requires the two to be equal. If f(c) = 5 but $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = 4$, both exist, yet the graph has a hole at height 4 with the point at height 5, so f is not continuous there (a removable discontinuity).
cards.h: → two conditions met → the third needs equality → limit ≠ value → a hole with a displaced point
cards.n: Listing only 'defined' and 'limit exists' as the definition is incomplete; the equality condition is the one most often left out.
o: The single equation lim f(x) = f(c) is the definition; existence of each side is necessary but not sufficient.
Counterexample: (x² − 4)/(x − 2) for x ≠ 2 with f(2) = 5 has limit 4 ≠ 5 at x = 2.

w.a: If f(c) is defined and the limit exists, f is continuous at c.
w.why: omits the equality condition

w.a: f is continuous if the graph has a point at x = c.
w.why: a displaced point is still a discontinuity

w.a: f is continuous at c because the limit is close to f(c).
w.why: close is not equal

cards.q: Explain why checking that the two formulas of a piecewise function give the same value at x = c is not, by itself, enough to show continuity at c.
cards.a: Matching formulas show the one-sided limits agree, so the limit exists. But f(c) may be defined by a separate line (say f(c) = 7), and continuity also needs f(c) to equal that limit. All three conditions must be checked: f(c), the limit, and their equality.
cards.h: → formulas agree → limit exists → f(c) may be defined separately → it must equal the limit
cards.n: 'The pieces meet, so it's continuous' earns nothing when f(c) is given on its own line; compare its value with the limit.
o: If f(x) = x² for x < 1, 2x − 1 for x > 1, and f(1) = 3, the pieces meet at height 1 but f(1) = 3, so f is not continuous at 1.
Agreement of the formulas settles condition 2 only; conditions 1 and 3 need f(c) itself.

w.a: If the two pieces meet at x = c, the function is always continuous there.
w.why: f(c) might be defined by a separate value

w.a: Continuity only needs the left and right formulas to agree.
w.why: it also needs f(c) to equal their common limit

w.a: If f(c) is defined, you don't need to check the one-sided limits.
w.why: the limit must exist and equal f(c)

cards.q: Explain why the justification 'f is continuous at 2 because f(2) = 4 and the graph passes through (2, 4)' earns no credit.
cards.a: It shows only condition 1, that f(2) is defined. Continuity needs $\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$ to exist and equal f(2); a graph can pass through (2, 4) as a displaced point while the curve approaches another height, or jump there. The justification must state lim f(x) = 4 = f(2).
cards.h: → only the value is given → the limit is not shown → a point can sit off the curve → state lim = f(2)
cards.n: Graders look for the limit equation; 'passes through the point' or 'no break in the graph' without it is not a justification.
o: A complete answer: f(2) = 4, the one-sided limits both equal 4, so lim f(x) = 4 = f(2), and f is continuous at x = 2.
A function with a jump at 2 and f(2) = 4 also 'passes through (2, 4)', so the statement cannot tell continuous from discontinuous.

w.a: It is continuous because there is a point at (2, 4).
w.why: a point alone does not show the limit

w.a: It is continuous because you can draw it without lifting the pencil.
w.why: an informal description, not the definition

w.a: It is continuous because f(2) exists.
w.why: existence is one of three conditions

cards.q: Explain what it means for f to be continuous on the closed interval [a, b].
cards.a: f is continuous at every point of the open interval (a, b), and one-sided continuous at the endpoints: $\lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x) = f(a)$ and $\lim_{x \to b^{-}} f(x) = f(b)$. Only the inward side matters at an endpoint, since f need not be defined outside [a, b].
cards.n: Continuity on the closed interval is the exact hypothesis the IVT (and later the EVT and MVT) requires; continuity on (a, b) alone is not enough.

cards.q: f is continuous on (0,3) and (3,6), with $\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to 3^{+}} f(x) = f(3) = 5$. Decide whether f is continuous on [0,6], and justify.
cards.a: Only continuity on (0, 6) follows. At x = 3 both one-sided limits equal 5 = f(3), so f is continuous at 3; with the two open pieces, f is continuous at every point of (0, 6). Continuity on [0, 6] also needs $\lim_{x \to 0^{+}} f(x) = f(0)$ and $\lim_{x \to 6^{-}} f(x) = f(6)$, which the information does not give.
cards.h: → check the shared point, then the two endpoints
cards.n: Answering 'yes' checks x = 3 but forgets the endpoints: [0, 6] needs one-sided continuity at 0 and at 6, and neither is stated.

cards.q:
Determine the interval(s) on which each function is continuous.
1. x⁴ − 3x + 2
2. (x + 1)/(x² − 9)
3. √(x − 4)
4. ln(x + 2)
5. eˣ/x
6. ∛x
7. tan x
8. 1/(x² + 1)
9. √(9 − x²)
10. ln(x²)
11. sec x
12. x^(3/2)
cards.a:
1 → (−∞, ∞): polynomial
2 → (−∞, −3), (−3, 3), (3, ∞): rational, denominator 0 at ±3
3 → [4, ∞): continuous from the right at 4
4 → (−2, ∞): log of a positive input
5 → (−∞, 0), (0, ∞)
6 → (−∞, ∞): an odd root is defined for all x
7 → each interval (−π/2 + kπ, π/2 + kπ), k an integer
8 → (−∞, ∞): the denominator is never 0
9 → [−3, 3]: one-sided continuity at both endpoints
10 → (−∞, 0), (0, ∞)
11 → each interval (−π/2 + kπ, π/2 + kπ), k an integer
12 → [0, ∞)
cards.h: → interval(s) + the domain reason, one per line
cards.n: Merging separate intervals into one, such as (−∞, ∞) for item 5, claims continuity at a point where the function is undefined.

cards.q: State the function families that are continuous at every point of their domains, and what this lets you conclude about limits.
cards.a: Polynomial, rational, power (including roots), exponential, logarithmic and trigonometric functions are continuous at every point of their domains; so are sums, differences, products, quotients (where the denominator ≠ 0) and compositions of them. So for any such f and any c in its domain, $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$.
cards.h: → families, combinations, then the limit consequence
cards.n: 'Continuous on its domain' is not 'continuous everywhere': 1/x is continuous on its domain but has no value, and no continuity, at x = 0.

cards.q: Determine where $f(x) = \frac{x+2}{x^{2}-x-6}$ is continuous, and justify.
cards.a: On (−∞, −2), (−2, 3) and (3, ∞). f is rational, so it is continuous at every point of its domain; x² − x − 6 = (x − 3)(x + 2) is 0 at x = 3 and x = −2, so those points are excluded: a hole at x = −2, where the factor cancels, and a vertical asymptote at x = 3.
cards.n: Cancelling x + 2 first and then reporting continuity at x = −2 is wrong: f is undefined there, and cancelling does not change the domain.

cards.q: Determine the intervals on which f is continuous, where f(x) = x² for x < 1, f(x) = 2x − 1 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3, and f(x) = 7 − x for x > 3.
cards.a: On (−∞, 3] and on (3, ∞). Each piece is a polynomial, continuous on its own interval. At x = 1: x² → 1 from the left, 2x − 1 → 1 from the right, and f(1) = 1, so f is continuous at 1. At x = 3: 2x − 1 → 5 from the left but 7 − x → 4 from the right, a jump. Since f(3) = 5 matches the left side, f is continuous from the left at 3.
cards.h: → each piece, then each boundary, then the intervals
cards.n: Checking the pieces but not the boundary points misses the jump at x = 3; the interval (−∞, 3] includes 3 because f(3) matches the left side.

cards.q: Determine whether g(x) = √(9 − x²) is continuous on [−3, 3], checking the endpoints.
cards.a: Yes. For −3 < x < 3, 9 − x² > 0, and g is a composition of a polynomial and the square root, each continuous on its domain, so g is continuous at every interior point. At the endpoints, $\lim_{x \to -3^{+}} g(x) = 0 = g(-3)$ and $\lim_{x \to 3^{-}} g(x) = 0 = g(3)$, so g is continuous from the inside at both ends.
cards.h: → interior reason, then one-sided checks at the ends
cards.n: Demanding two-sided limits at x = ±3 is the error: g is undefined outside [−3, 3], and an endpoint needs only one-sided continuity.

cards.q: Determine whether f(x) = 1/x is continuous on its domain, and whether it is continuous on [−1, 1].
cards.a: It is continuous on its domain, (−∞, 0) and (0, ∞): it is rational, so it is continuous at every point where it is defined. It is not continuous on [−1, 1], because 0 is in [−1, 1] and f(0) is undefined (there is a vertical asymptote at x = 0). Continuity on an interval needs continuity at every point of the interval.
cards.h: → two verdicts, each with its reason
cards.n: '1/x is continuous' with no interval named is ambiguous; on any interval containing 0 it fails, which blocks the IVT there.

cards.q: Explain why continuity of each piece of a piecewise function on its own interval does not guarantee continuity on the whole domain.
cards.a: Each formula's continuity covers only the open interval where it is used. At a boundary point the function switches formulas, so continuity there needs its own check: the one-sided limits (from different formulas) must agree and equal f(c). A mismatch creates a jump even though every piece is continuous.
cards.h: → pieces continuous inside their intervals → boundaries use two formulas → check the limits and f(c) there
cards.n: 'Each piece is a polynomial, so f is continuous everywhere' earns nothing without the boundary check.
o: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2 and x² for x ≥ 2 has polynomial pieces but a jump at x = 2 (3 versus 4).
Continuity on an interval means continuity at every point of it, and the boundary points are points of the interval.

w.a: Since each piece is continuous, the whole function is continuous.
w.why: the boundaries need their own check

w.a: A piecewise function is never continuous at a boundary.
w.why: it is continuous when the limits match f(c)

w.a: You only need f(c) to be defined at the boundary.
w.why: the one-sided limits must also agree with it

cards.q: Explain why tan x is continuous on (−π/2, π/2) but not on [0, π].
cards.a: tan x = sin x/cos x is continuous wherever cos x ≠ 0. On (−π/2, π/2), cos x > 0, so tan x is continuous at every point. But [0, π] contains π/2, where cos x = 0 and tan x is undefined, with a vertical asymptote; continuity on an interval fails if it fails at any one point.
cards.h: → tan is continuous where cos ≠ 0 → (−π/2, π/2) avoids zeros of cos → [0, π] contains π/2 → fails there
cards.n: 'Trig functions are continuous' is not a reason; they are continuous on their domains, and π/2 is not in the domain of tan.
o: tan x is a quotient of continuous functions, continuous except where its denominator cos x is 0, which on [0, π] happens at x = π/2.
Near π/2 the one-sided limits of tan x are +∞ and −∞, an infinite discontinuity inside [0, π].

w.a: tan x is continuous everywhere because it is a trig function.
w.why: it is undefined where cos x = 0

w.a: tan x is not continuous on [0, π] because tan π = 0.
w.why: a zero value is not a discontinuity

w.a: tan x is continuous on [0, π] because it is defined at both endpoints.
w.why: the problem is the interior point π/2

cards.q: Explain why only one-sided limits are checked at the endpoints when showing continuity on a closed interval [a, b].
