cards.a: 1. $\lim_{a \to -\infty} \left[e^{x}\right]_{a}^{0} = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left(1 - e^{a}\right) = 1$, since $e^{a} \to 0$ as a → −∞.
cards.h: → limit at the lower end, then the value
cards.n: BC only. Here the lower limit is the infinite one, so the limit variable runs to −∞; a limit at the upper end sets up a different integral.

cards.q: Evaluate $\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^{2/3}} dx$, which has an interior discontinuity at x=0.
cards.a: 6. Split at 0: $\int_{-1}^{0} x^{-2/3}\,dx + \int_{0}^{1} x^{-2/3}\,dx$. The right piece is $\lim_{a \to 0^{+}} \left[3x^{1/3}\right]_{a}^{1} = 3$; the left is $\lim_{c \to 0^{-}} \left[3x^{1/3}\right]_{-1}^{c} = 0 - (-3) = 3$. Both converge, so the total is 6.
cards.n: BC only. Integrating straight through happens to give 6 here, but only because both pieces converge; the split with limits is what earns the point.

cards.q: Evaluate $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{1+x^{2}}\,dx$.
cards.a: π. Split at 0: $\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} = \lim_{b \to \infty} \arctan b = \frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{0} \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} = \lim_{a \to -\infty} \left(0 - \arctan a\right) = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Both converge, so the integral is π.
cards.h: → split at 0, a limit for each end, add
cards.n: BC only. One symmetric limit, $\lim_{b \to \infty} \int_{-b}^{b}$, is not the definition; each infinite end needs its own limit.

cards.q: Evaluate $\int_{0}^{\infty} xe^{-x}\,dx$.
cards.a: 1. By parts, $\int_{0}^{b} xe^{-x}\,dx = \left[-xe^{-x} - e^{-x}\right]_{0}^{b} = 1 - be^{-b} - e^{-b}$. As b → ∞, $e^{-b} \to 0$ and $\frac{b}{e^{b}} \to 0$ by L'Hospital's Rule ($\frac{1}{e^{b}} \to 0$). So the integral converges to 1.
cards.h: → parts on [0, b], then the limit
cards.n: BC only. Calling $be^{-b}$ '∞ · 0 = 0' skips the limit work; L'Hospital's Rule (borrowed from Unit 4) settles it.

cards.q: Decide whether $\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx$ converges, and if so, find its value.
cards.a: Converges, to 2. The integrand is unbounded at 0, so $\int_{0}^{1} x^{-1/2}\,dx = \lim_{a \to 0^{+}} \left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_{a}^{1} = \lim_{a \to 0^{+}} \left(2 - 2\sqrt{a}\right) = 2$, a finite limit.
cards.h: → unbounded at 0 → lim as a → 0⁺ of ∫ from a to 1 → 2 − 2√a → 2 → converges
cards.n: BC only. 'Diverges because of the asymptote at 0' is the trap: an unbounded integrand can still enclose finite area.
o: On [0, 1] a p-integral converges when p < 1, and here p = 1/2.
The antiderivative 2√x stays bounded near 0, so the accumulated area from a to 1 levels off as a → 0⁺.

w.a: Diverges, because $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$ has a vertical asymptote at 0.
w.why: an asymptote alone does not decide it

w.a: Diverges, because p = 1/2 < 1.
w.why: p < 1 means divergence on [1, ∞), convergence on [0, 1]

w.a: Converges to 2, since $\left[2\sqrt{x}\right]_{0}^{1} = 2$.
w.why: right value, but it needs the limit as a → 0⁺

cards.q: Decide whether $\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{x^{2}}\,dx$ converges or diverges.
cards.a: Diverges. The integrand is unbounded at 0, so $\int_{0}^{1} x^{-2}\,dx = \lim_{a \to 0^{+}} \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{a}^{1} = \lim_{a \to 0^{+}} \left(\frac{1}{a} - 1\right) = \infty$. The limit is not finite.
cards.h: → unbounded at 0 → lim as a → 0⁺ of ∫ from a to 1 → 1/a − 1 → ∞ → diverges
cards.n: BC only. For $\int_{0}^{1} x^{-p}\,dx$ the threshold is reversed from [1, ∞): it converges only for p < 1, and here p = 2.
o: On [0, 1] a p-integral with p ≥ 1 diverges, and here p = 2.
Near 0 the antiderivative −1/x is unbounded, so the area from a to 1 grows without bound as a → 0⁺.

w.a: Converges, because p = 2 > 1.
w.why: p > 1 is the test on [1, ∞), not on [0, 1]

w.a: It converges to −1, the value of $-\frac{1}{x}$ at x = 1.
w.why: the lower-limit term 1/a is unbounded, not 0

w.a: It diverges, because $\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ is undefined at x = 0.
w.why: an undefined endpoint alone decides nothing; the integral of 1/√x on [0, 1] converges

cards.q: Decide whether $\int_{0}^{\infty} \cos x dx$ converges.
cards.a: It diverges. $\int_{0}^{b} \cos x\,dx = \sin b$, and $\lim_{b \to \infty} \sin b$ does not exist: sin b keeps oscillating between −1 and 1. An improper integral converges only when its limit exists and is finite.
cards.h: → ∫ from 0 to b = sin b → sin b oscillates → no limit → diverges
cards.n: BC only. Divergence does not require growing to infinity; a limit that keeps oscillating also fails to exist.
o: The humps of cos x never shrink, so the accumulated area keeps swinging between −1 and 1 without settling.
b = 2πk gives the value 0 and b = π/2 + 2πk gives 1, so no single limiting value exists.

w.a: It converges to 0, because the positive and negative areas cancel.
w.why: they cancel only at some b; the limit does not exist

w.a: It converges, because cos x is bounded.
w.why: a bounded integrand can still give a divergent integral

w.a: It diverges to ∞.
w.why: sin b stays between −1 and 1; it diverges by oscillation

cards.q: Explain why $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,dx$ diverges even though $\int_{-b}^{b} x\,dx = 0$ for every b.
cards.a: With two infinite limits the integral is split, $\int_{-\infty}^{0} x\,dx + \int_{0}^{\infty} x\,dx$, and each piece needs its own limit. $\int_{0}^{b} x\,dx = \frac{b^{2}}{2} \to \infty$, so that piece diverges, and one divergent piece makes the whole integral diverge.
cards.h: → split at 0 → ∫ from 0 to b = b²/2 → ∞ → one piece diverges → the whole integral diverges
cards.n: BC only. Answering 0 'by symmetry' uses one symmetric limit, which is not how an integral over (−∞, ∞) is defined.
o: Taking the ends at different rates, $\int_{-b}^{2b} x\,dx = \frac{3b^{2}}{2} \to \infty$, gives a different result, so no single value exists.
The graph of y = x encloses infinite area on each side of 0, and ∞ − ∞ has no value.

w.a: It converges to 0, because x is an odd function.
w.why: symmetry cancels only when each half converges

w.a: It converges, because the areas on the two sides are equal.
w.why: both areas are infinite

w.a: It diverges, because x is not continuous everywhere.
w.why: x is continuous; the areas are infinite

cards.q: Explain why $\int_{1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{x}\,dx$ diverges even though $\frac{1}{x} \to 0$ as x → ∞.
cards.a: $\int_{1}^{b} \frac{1}{x}\,dx = \ln b$, and ln b → ∞ as b → ∞, so the limit is not finite and the integral diverges. The integrand does approach 0, but too slowly: the area from 1 to b keeps growing without bound.
cards.h: → ∫ from 1 to b = ln b → ln b → ∞ → diverges; 1/x → 0 too slowly
cards.n: BC only. 'The function goes to 0, so the area is finite' is the classic wrong argument; $\frac{1}{x^{2}}$ goes to 0 fast enough, $\frac{1}{x}$ does not.
o: It is the p-integral with p = 1, the boundary case, which diverges.
Each doubling of the interval, from b to 2b, adds ln 2 more area, so the total never levels off.

w.a: It converges, because 1/x approaches 0.
w.why: an integrand tending to 0 does not guarantee convergence

w.a: It converges to 1, because p = 1.
w.why: p = 1 is the divergent boundary case

w.a: It diverges, because 1/x is undefined at 0.
w.why: x = 0 is outside [1, ∞)

cards.q: Give a decision order for choosing an antidifferentiation technique.
cards.a: 1) A basic antiderivative, possibly after algebra (expand, split a fraction, cancel). 2) Substitution, if an inner function's derivative is a factor. 3) For a rational function: long division if improper, completing the square for an irreducible quadratic, linear partial fractions (BC) for distinct linear factors. 4) Integration by parts (BC) for a product of unlike types.
cards.n: Reaching for parts or partial fractions before algebra and substitution wastes time; most AB items fall to steps 1 and 2.

cards.q: Identify the technique for $\int \frac{2x+1}{x^{2}+x+7}\,dx$.
cards.a: Substitution with u = x² + x + 7: du = (2x + 1) dx is exactly the numerator, so the integral is $\int \frac{du}{u} = \ln(x^{2}+x+7) + C$, with no bars needed since x² + x + 7 > 0.
cards.n: Check numerator-equals-derivative-of-denominator first; partial fractions cannot even start, since x² + x + 7 has no real zeros.

cards.q: Decide the antidifferentiation technique for $\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}+9}}\,dx$, then evaluate it.
cards.a: Substitution; the result is $\sqrt{x^{2}+9} + C$. With u = x² + 9, du = 2x dx, so $x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}du$ and the integral is $\frac{1}{2}\int u^{-1/2}\,du = u^{1/2} + C$.
cards.n: Without the lone x in the numerator this would need a trigonometric substitution, which is outside the course; the x is the signal.

cards.q: Identify the technique for $\int \frac{3}{x^{2}-9} dx$, then evaluate it.
cards.a: Linear partial fractions (BC). x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), so $\frac{3}{x^{2}-9} = \frac{1/2}{x-3} - \frac{1/2}{x+3}$, and the integral is $\frac{1}{2}\ln|x-3| - \frac{1}{2}\ln|x+3| + C$.
cards.n: BC only. Reaching for arctangent because of the x² is the trap: x² − 9 has real zeros, and only x² + a² leads to an arctangent.

cards.q: Identify the technique for $\int x\sec^{2}x dx$, then set up (but do not finish) the first step.
cards.a: Integration by parts (BC): u = x and dv = sec²x dx, so du = dx and v = tan x, giving $x\tan x - \int \tan x\,dx$. (Finished: x tan x + ln|cos x| + C.)
cards.h: → technique, u and dv, the first step
cards.n: BC only. Taking u = sec²x makes v = $\frac{x^{2}}{2}$ and the new integral needs $\frac{x^{2}}{2} \cdot 2\sec^{2}x\tan x$, which is worse.

cards.q: Decide the first move for $\int \frac{x^{2}-1}{x+1} dx$, before reaching for any named integration technique.
cards.a: Factor and cancel: $\frac{x^{2}-1}{x+1} = \frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x+1} = x - 1$ for x ≠ −1, so the integral is $\frac{x^{2}}{2} - x + C$.
cards.n: Long division gives the same quotient x − 1 with remainder 0; substitution or partial fractions would be wasted effort.

cards.q:
Identify the technique that finishes each integral (basic rule after algebra, substitution, long division, completing the square, parts, or partial fractions), and give the antiderivative.
1. $\int x^{2}e^{x^{3}}\,dx$
2. $\int x^{2}e^{x}\,dx$
3. $\int \frac{x+1}{x}\,dx$
4. $\int \frac{1}{x^{2}+2x+10}\,dx$
5. $\int \frac{1}{x^{2}+2x-3}\,dx$
6. $\int \frac{x^{3}}{x^{2}+1}\,dx$
7. $\int \sin x\cos x\,dx$
8. $\int x\ln x\,dx$
9. $\int \frac{\cos x}{1+\sin^{2} x}\,dx$
10. $\int \frac{2x}{x^{2}-4}\,dx$
cards.a:
1 → substitution, u = x³: $\frac{1}{3}e^{x^{3}} + C$
2 → parts twice (BC): $(x^{2} - 2x + 2)e^{x} + C$
3 → algebra, $1 + \frac{1}{x}$: x + ln|x| + C
4 → complete the square, (x + 1)² + 9: $\frac{1}{3}\arctan\left(\frac{x+1}{3}\right) + C$
5 → partial fractions (BC), (x + 3)(x − 1): $\frac{1}{4}\ln|x-1| - \frac{1}{4}\ln|x+3| + C$
6 → long division, $x - \frac{x}{x^{2}+1}$: $\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\ln(x^{2}+1) + C$
7 → substitution, u = sin x: $\frac{1}{2}\sin^{2} x + C$
8 → parts (BC), u = ln x: $\frac{x^{2}}{2}\ln x - \frac{x^{2}}{4} + C$
9 → substitution, u = sin x: arctan(sin x) + C
10 → substitution, u = x² − 4: ln|x² − 4| + C
cards.n: Case 10 looks like partial fractions, but its numerator is the denominator's derivative, so substitution takes one line. Parts and partial fractions are BC only.

cards.q:
Find each integral. They look alike but need different methods.
1. $\int \frac{x}{x^{2}+1}\,dx$
2. $\int \frac{1}{x^{2}+1}\,dx$
3. $\int \frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}\,dx$
4. $\int \frac{2}{x^{2}-1}\,dx$
5. $\int \frac{x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}\,dx$
6. $\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx$
cards.a:
1 → $\frac{1}{2}\ln(x^{2}+1) + C$ (substitution, u = x² + 1)
2 → arctan x + C (basic)
3 → x − arctan x + C (division: $1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}+1}$)
4 → ln|x − 1| − ln|x + 1| + C (partial fractions, BC)
5 → $-\frac{1}{2(x^{2}+1)} + C$ (substitution, u = x² + 1)
6 → $-\sqrt{1-x^{2}} + C$ (substitution, u = 1 − x²; not arcsin)
cards.h: → one antiderivative per line, with its method
cards.n: Answering arctan x for case 1 or ½ ln(x² + 1) for case 2 swaps the two most common look-alikes; an x in the numerator signals substitution.

cards.q: Contrast when you would use u-substitution versus integration by parts.
cards.a: Substitution when the integrand is a composite times its inner derivative, up to a constant: $\int 2x\cos(x^{2})\,dx$. Parts (BC) when it is a product of unrelated factors with no such pattern and differentiating one factor simplifies it: $\int x\cos x\,dx$ with u = x.
cards.h: → inner derivative present → substitution; unrelated product, one factor simplifies → parts
cards.n: Parts on $\int 2x\cos(x^{2})\,dx$ leads to a harder integral; test for the derivative pattern first. Parts is BC only.
o: Substitution reverses the chain rule and parts reverses the product rule, so ask which rule would have produced the integrand.
In $\int xe^{x^{2}}\,dx$ the x is half the derivative of x², so substitute; in $\int xe^{x}\,dx$ it is not, so use parts.

w.a: Use parts whenever the integrand is a product.
w.why: products like 2x cos(x²) are substitution problems

w.a: Use substitution only when there is a square root.
w.why: any composite with its inner derivative qualifies

w.a: They are interchangeable; either one always works.
w.why: each fails where the other succeeds

cards.q: Explain why $\int \frac{1}{x^{2}+4}\,dx$ is not found with partial fractions but $\int \frac{1}{x^{2}-4}\,dx$ is.
cards.a: Partial fractions needs real linear factors. x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2), so $\frac{1}{x^{2}-4} = \frac{1/4}{x-2} - \frac{1/4}{x+2}$, a sum of logarithms. x² + 4 is always positive and has no real factors; it matches the arctangent form: $\frac{1}{2}\arctan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) + C$.
cards.h: → x² − 4 factors into distinct linear factors → logs; x² + 4 has no real zeros → arctan
cards.n: Writing the factors of x² + 4 with i is outside the course; a sum x² + a² in the denominator signals the arctangent. Partial fractions is BC only.
o: The second integral is $\frac{1}{4}\ln\left|\frac{x-2}{x+2}\right| + C$, and the first differentiates back from $\frac{1}{2}\arctan\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$.
The discriminant decides: x² − 4 has two real zeros, x² + 4 has none.

w.a: Both use partial fractions, because both denominators are quadratics.
w.why: x² + 4 has no real linear factors

w.a: Both are arctangents, because both have x² and 4.
w.why: x² − 4 factors, so it gives logarithms

w.a: The first is $\ln(x^{2}+4) + C$.
w.why: that needs a numerator 2x

cards.q: Define a differential equation.
cards.a: An equation relating an unknown function to one or more of its derivatives, e.g. $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2xy$. A solution is a FUNCTION, not a number.
cards.h: → definition plus what a solution is
cards.n: The order is the highest derivative that appears, and BC only requires solving first-order separable equations.

cards.q: Translate 'the rate of change of y is directly proportional to y' into a differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$ for some constant k.
cards.n: 'Proportional to' always introduces an unnamed constant k; do not assume k = 1.

cards.q: Write Newton's Law of Cooling as a differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dT}{dt} = k\left(T - T_{s}\right)$, where $T_{s}$ is the surrounding temperature and k < 0 for cooling.
cards.n: The solution has the form $T = T_{s} + Ce^{kt}$.

cards.q: Explain how to verify that a given function is a solution of a differential equation.
cards.a: Differentiate the candidate, substitute it and its derivative into BOTH sides of the equation, and simplify to show the sides are identical for all x in the domain.
cards.n: Show the substitution explicitly; asserting it works earns nothing.

cards.q: Contrast a general solution with a particular solution.
cards.a: A general solution contains the arbitrary constant C and names an entire family of curves. A particular solution uses an initial condition to pin down C, giving one curve.
cards.n: Apply the initial condition right after integrating, before solving for y; the algebra stays much simpler that way.

cards.q: Define a slope field.
cards.a: A grid of short line segments; the segment at (x, y) has slope $\frac{dy}{dx}$ evaluated there. It shows the shape of every solution curve without solving the equation.
cards.n: A solution curve follows the segments and never crosses another solution curve, so curves cannot merge or touch.

cards.q: Give a strategy for matching a slope field to its differential equation.
cards.a: Test special locations: where are segments horizontal (dy/dx = 0)? Do slopes depend only on x (columns identical) or only on y (rows identical)? Check the sign in each quadrant.
cards.n: Rows identical (same slope all along a horizontal row) means dy/dx depends only on y; columns identical means it depends only on x.

cards.q: Explain how to sketch a particular solution curve on a slope field through a given point.
cards.a: Start at the point and draw a smooth curve that stays TANGENT to the segments it passes, following them left and right; do not cross other solution curves and do not leave the given grid.
cards.n: Curves must pass through the marked point and follow, not connect, the segments.

cards.q: Explain how to spot equilibrium solutions from a slope field or a differential equation.
cards.a: Set $\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$ and solve for constant y values; on the field these appear as full horizontal rows of flat segments. Those constants are equilibrium solutions.
cards.n: Only constant solutions qualify; a curve that merely has slope zero at one isolated point is not an equilibrium.

cards.q: State Euler's method update formulas.
cards.a: $x_{n+1} = x_{n} + h$ and $y_{n+1} = y_{n} + h \cdot \frac{dy}{dx}$ evaluated at $(x_{n}, y_{n})$; h is the step size.
cards.n: This is repeated local linearization, one tangent-line step at a time.

cards.q: Explain how to choose the step size h in Euler's method.
cards.a: Divide the total change in x by the number of steps: h = (target x minus start x) / (number of steps). h is negative when stepping to the left of the initial point.
cards.n: Backward steps with negative h are a favorite MC twist.

cards.q: Predict whether Euler's method over- or underestimates the true solution.
cards.a: Concave up solution: Euler UNDERestimates (tangent lines lie below). Concave down: Euler OVERestimates. Determine concavity from the sign of $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$.
cards.n: Same logic as tangent-line approximation, applied repeatedly.

cards.q: Explain the effect of decreasing the step size in Euler's method.
cards.a: Smaller h means more steps and less error, since each tangent-line segment departs from the curve for a shorter distance. The approximation approaches the true solution as h approaches 0.
cards.n: Euler underestimates a concave up solution and overestimates a concave down one, since each step rides a tangent line.

cards.q: Name the most common Euler's method bookkeeping error.
cards.a: Evaluating the slope with the NEW x but the OLD y (or vice versa). The slope for each step must use the point at the START of that step.
cards.n: Keep an x, y, dy/dx, new y table and fill it row by row.

cards.q: Explain the separation of variables procedure.
cards.a: Write $\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)g(y)$, move all y terms with dy to one side and all x terms with dx to the other, integrate both sides, put a single +C on the x side, then solve for y.
cards.n: If dy/dx cannot be factored into f(x)g(y), the equation is not separable.

cards.q: State the test for whether a differential equation is separable.
cards.a: It is separable exactly when $\frac{dy}{dx}$ can be written as a PRODUCT f(x)g(y). Sums like $\frac{dy}{dx} = x + y$ are not separable.
cards.n: Grouping can expose a hidden product, as in $\frac{dy}{dx}=xy+x=x(y+1)$, which is separable after all.

cards.q: Explain where the constant of integration goes when separating variables.
cards.a: Add a single C to one side only (conventionally the x side) after integrating; two constants would just combine into one.
cards.n: Forgetting C entirely makes the initial condition unusable.

cards.q: Explain how the absolute value from $\int \frac{1}{y}\,dy$ is handled.
cards.a: Integrating gives $\ln|y|$; exponentiating gives $|y| = e^{C}e^{kx}$, and the sign is absorbed into a new constant so $y = Ce^{kx}$ with C allowed to be negative.
cards.n: On AP responses you may go straight to $y = Ce^{kx}$.

cards.q: Explain the correct order of steps when an initial condition is given.
cards.a: Separate and integrate, substitute the initial condition to solve for C IMMEDIATELY, then solve for y. Solving for y first makes the algebra much worse.
cards.n: This is the standard AP free-response sequence.

cards.q: Explain how the initial condition determines the sign when solving $y^{2} = $ something for y.
cards.a: Take the branch whose sign matches the initial y value: if y(0) = -3, keep the negative square root. Solutions cannot jump branches.
cards.n: Choosing the wrong root is a routine lost point.

cards.q: State the domain convention for a particular solution to a differential equation.
cards.a: The domain is the largest interval containing the initial x value on which the solution is defined and differentiable — it stops at any vertical asymptote or endpoint of validity.
cards.n: The interval may not jump across an asymptote even when the formula still returns values on the far side.

cards.q: State the exponential growth and decay model and its solution.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$ has solution $y = y_{0}e^{kt}$, where $y_{0}$ is the initial amount; k > 0 is growth, k < 0 is decay.
cards.n: Separating variables on dy/dt = ky is the standard derivation; know it both ways.

cards.q: Explain how to find the doubling time for exponential growth.
cards.a: Solve $2y_{0} = y_{0}e^{kt}$, giving $t = \frac{\ln 2}{k}$. It does not depend on the starting amount.
cards.n: The same form covers any fixed multiple, so tripling time is $\frac{\ln 3}{k}$ by the identical algebra.

cards.q: Explain how to find the half-life for exponential decay.
cards.a: Solve $\frac{1}{2}y_{0} = y_{0}e^{kt}$, giving $t = \frac{\ln(0.5)}{k} = -\frac{\ln 2}{k}$, positive because k < 0.
cards.n: Report a half-life as a positive time; the negative sign belongs to k, which is negative for decay.

cards.q: Explain what the constant k means in $\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$.
cards.a: k is the relative (per-unit) growth rate: $k = \frac{1}{y}\frac{dy}{dt}$, the fractional change per unit time. Its units are 1 over time.
cards.n: Because k alone sets doubling time and half-life, two populations of very different size can share both.

cards.q: State the logistic differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dP}{dt} = kP\left(1 - \frac{P}{L}\right)$, where k > 0 and L is the carrying capacity.
cards.n: Also written $\frac{dP}{dt} = kP - \frac{k}{L}P^{2}$.

cards.q: Define carrying capacity in a logistic model.
cards.a: The value L that the population approaches as $t \to \infty$; it is the nonzero equilibrium solution where $\frac{dP}{dt} = 0$.
cards.n: Also the horizontal asymptote of the logistic curve.

cards.q: Identify where a logistic population grows FASTEST.
cards.a: At $P = \frac{L}{2}$, half the carrying capacity. That is where $\frac{dP}{dt}$ is maximized and where the logistic curve has its inflection point.
cards.n: Maximize dP/dt by setting its derivative with respect to P equal to zero.

cards.q: State $\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t)$ for a logistic model with 0 < P(0) < L.
cards.a: L, the carrying capacity.
cards.n: True for any positive starting population; if P(0) > L the population decreases to L.

cards.q: Identify the equilibrium solutions of the logistic differential equation.
cards.a: P = 0 and P = L. P = 0 is unstable; P = L is stable (solutions on both sides move toward it).
cards.n: Justify stability by the sign of dP/dt on each side, so test one P between 0 and L and one above L.

cards.q: Explain how to read k and L directly from $\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.04P - 0.0002P^{2}$.
cards.a: Factor: $0.04P\left(1 - \frac{0.0002}{0.04}P\right)$, so k = 0.04 and $\frac{1}{L} = \frac{0.0002}{0.04}$, giving L = 200.
cards.n: Shortcut: L is the ratio of the linear coefficient to the quadratic coefficient.

cards.q: Describe the shape of the logistic solution curve for $0 < P(0) < \frac{L}{2}$.
cards.a: S-shaped: increasing throughout, concave up below $P = \frac{L}{2}$, concave down above it, with an inflection at $P = \frac{L}{2}$ and horizontal asymptote P = L.
cards.n: If P(0) already exceeds $\frac{L}{2}$ the S shape never appears; the curve is concave down from the start.

cards.q: Contrast the long-run behavior of exponential and logistic growth models.
cards.a: Exponential growth increases without bound. Logistic growth slows as P nears L and levels off at the carrying capacity.
cards.n: Logistic behaves like exponential when P is small compared with L.

cards.q: State the general form of the solution to the logistic differential equation.
cards.a: $P(t) = \frac{L}{1 + Ae^{-kt}}$, where A is fixed by the initial condition.
cards.n: BC students are not required to derive it, but recognizing the form is worth easy MC points.

cards.q: Predict the sign of $\frac{dP}{dt}$ for a logistic model when 0 < P < L and when P > L.
cards.a: Positive for 0 < P < L (population grows) and negative for P > L (population falls back toward L).
cards.n: P = 0 and P = L both make dP/dt zero, so no solution curve ever crosses either of those horizontal lines.

cards.q: State the AP Calculus rounding convention on the calculator-active sections.
cards.a: Report decimal approximations to at least THREE places after the decimal point, truncated or rounded. Store full precision in the calculator and round only at the very end.
cards.n: Rounding intermediate values is a classic silent point loss on multi-part free-response.

cards.q: Use Euler's method with step size 0.5 to estimate y(1) if y'=x+y, y(0)=1.
cards.n: Recompute the slope x+y at the NEW point every step; reusing the old slope is the top Euler's method error.

cards.q: Use Euler's method with step size 0.1 to estimate y(0.2) if $\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy$, y(0)=1.
cards.n: Each new slope is evaluated at the point just computed; reusing the starting slope is the most common Euler error.

cards.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x}{y}$ with y(0)=3, and give y explicitly.
cards.a: $y=\sqrt{x^{2}+9}$. Separate to $y\,dy=x\,dx$, integrate to $\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\frac{x^{2}}{2}+C$, use y(0)=3 to get $y^{2}=x^{2}+9$, then take the positive root since y(0)=3>0.
cards.n: Squaring hides a second branch, and it is the positive initial value y(0)=3 that selects the plus root.

cards.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=3y$ with y(0)=2, and give y explicitly.
cards.a: $y=2e^{3x}$. Separate to $\frac{dy}{y}=3\,dx$, integrate to $\ln|y|=3x+C$, exponentiate to $y=Ae^{3x}$, then use y(0)=2 to find A=2.
cards.n: The proportional form lets you jump to $y=Ae^{3x}$, but write the separation anyway to earn the setup points.

cards.q: Find the general solution to $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}$ for x>0.
cards.a: y=Ax for a constant A. Separate to $\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{dx}{x}$, integrate both sides to $\ln|y|=\ln|x|+C$, then exponentiate.
cards.n: The restriction x > 0 is what lets $\ln|x|$ be written as $\ln x$; the family otherwise splits at the origin.

cards.q: A slope field for $\frac{dy}{dx}=y-2$ shows horizontal segments along one line. Identify that line and explain why.
cards.a: y = 2. The slope $\frac{dy}{dx}=y-2$ equals 0 exactly when y=2, so every segment drawn along that horizontal line has zero slope.
cards.n: That line is also the equilibrium solution of the differential equation.

cards.q: For $\frac{dy}{dx}=x-y$, find the slope of the segment the slope field draws at the point (2,1).
cards.a: 1. Substitute the point directly into the differential equation: at (2,1), $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2-1 = 1$.
cards.n: Nothing is solved here; the differential equation already is a formula for the slope at whatever point you plug in.

cards.q: A population grows exponentially from 200 to 350 in 5 years. Predict the population after 10 years.
cards.n: Squaring $e^{5k}$ avoids solving for k explicitly — doubling the elapsed time squares the growth factor.

cards.q: For the logistic model $\frac{dP}{dt}=0.02P\left(1-\frac{P}{500}\right)$, find the carrying capacity and the population at which growth is fastest.
cards.a: Carrying capacity L=500; growth is fastest at P=250 (half of L), the inflection point of the logistic curve.
cards.n: Read L from the denominator inside $1-\frac{P}{L}$; the leading 0.02 is k and has nothing to do with capacity.

cards.q: Verify that $y=3e^{2x}$ is a solution of $\frac{dy}{dx}=2y$.
cards.a: Yes. Differentiating gives $y'=6e^{2x}$, and $2y=2\left(3e^{2x}\right)=6e^{2x}$, so the two sides agree for every x.
cards.h: → yes or no, with both sides
cards.n: The coefficient 3 plays no role, since every constant multiple of $e^{2x}$ satisfies this equation.

cards.q: Write a differential equation for a population P(t) that increases at a rate proportional to the SQUARE ROOT of P.
cards.a: $\frac{dP}{dt}=k\sqrt{P}$ for some positive constant k. 'Proportional to' translates directly into a constant multiple of the described quantity.
cards.n: Say explicitly that k is a positive constant; leaving k unknown is expected, but its sign must match growth.

cards.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}$ with y(3)=-4, and give y explicitly.
cards.a: $y=-\sqrt{25-x^{2}}$. Separate and integrate to $y^{2}=25-x^{2}$, then choose the NEGATIVE square root because y(3)=-4 is negative.
cards.n: The initial condition's sign, not the algebra, decides which branch of the square root to keep.

cards.q: A cup of coffee at 190°F is placed in a 70°F room, satisfying $\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-70)$. If it cools to 150°F after 10 minutes, compute k.
cards.a: $k=\frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{3}{2} \approx 0.041$. Solving gives $T(t)=70+120e^{-kt}$, and substituting T(10)=150 gives $e^{-10k}=\frac{80}{120}=\frac{2}{3}$, so $k=-\frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{3}{2}$.
cards.n: Reporting k as negative is the usual slip, since the minus sign is already written into the model itself.

cards.q: Write a differential equation modeling: a rumor spreads through a fixed population N at a rate proportional to the product of those who heard it, y, and those who have not, N-y.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dt}=ky(N-y)$ for some positive constant k. This proportional-to-a-product structure is exactly the logistic growth pattern.
cards.n: Leaving it factored as $ky(N-y)$ rather than expanding keeps the equilibria y = 0 and y = N in plain sight.

cards.q: Verify that $y=5-3e^{-2x}$ is a solution of $\frac{dy}{dx}=2(5-y)$.
cards.a: Differentiating gives $\frac{dy}{dx}=6e^{-2x}$. Substituting y into the right side gives $2(5-(5-3e^{-2x}))=2(3e^{-2x})=6e^{-2x}$, which matches, confirming it is a solution.
cards.n: Verifying a solution means substituting into BOTH sides of the original equation, not just checking it looks similar in form.

cards.q: A slope field has slope zero on both axes, positive in quadrants I and III, negative in quadrants II and IV. Identify a differential equation matching this pattern.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx}=xy$. The product xy is zero exactly on the axes, positive when x and y share a sign (quadrants I and III), and negative when they have opposite signs (quadrants II and IV).
cards.n: The answer is not unique; any equation with the same sign pattern, such as $\frac{dy}{dx}=3xy$, matches as well.

cards.q: A slope field for $\frac{dy}{dx}=1-y$ shows curves drawn toward the line y=1 from both above and below. Decide whether y=1 is a stable or unstable equilibrium, and justify.
cards.a: Stable. Below y=1, 1−y>0 so solutions increase toward it; above y=1, 1−y<0 so solutions decrease toward it — nearby solutions approach y=1 from both directions.
cards.n: Justify by testing the sign of dy/dx just above and just below the line, not by describing the drawn picture.

cards.q: Find the general solution to $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x^{2}}{y^{2}}$.
cards.a: $y=\left(x^{3}+C\right)^{1/3}$. Separating gives $y^{2}\,dy=x^{2}\,dx$, and integrating both sides gives $\frac{y^{3}}{3}=\frac{x^{3}}{3}+C_{1}$, which rearranges to $y^{3}=x^{3}+C$.
cards.n: Always add the constant of integration once, after combining both sides — not one on each side separately.

cards.q: Find the general solution to $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\cos x}{y}$.
cards.a: $y^{2}=2\sin x + C$. Separating gives $y\,dy=\cos x\,dx$, and integrating both sides gives $\frac{y^{2}}{2}=\sin x + C_{1}$, which rearranges to $y^{2}=2\sin x+C$.
cards.n: Leaving the answer in $y^{2}$ form is fine when no initial condition picks a branch of the square root.

cards.q: Solve $\frac{dy}{dx}=y\cos x$ with y(0)=2, and give y explicitly.
cards.a: $y=2e^{\sin x}$. Separating gives $\frac{dy}{y}=\cos x\,dx$, so $\ln|y|=\sin x+C$, meaning $y=Ae^{\sin x}$; the initial condition y(0)=2 gives A=2.
cards.n: Since y(0)=2 is positive, the solution stays positive for every x and the absolute value bars simply drop away.

cards.q: A radioactive sample decays at a rate proportional to the amount present, from 80 grams to 50 grams in 6 hours. Compute the amount remaining after a total of 12 hours.
cards.a: 31.25 grams. Since $A(t)=80e^{kt}$ with $e^{6k}=\frac{50}{80}=\frac{5}{8}$, the amount at t=12 is $80\left(e^{6k}\right)^{2}=80\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)^{2}=80\cdot\frac{25}{64}=31.25$.
cards.n: Keep the fraction $\frac{5}{8}$ exact through the squaring; rounding k early visibly shifts the final answer.

cards.q: For the logistic model $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\frac{P}{L}\right)$, show why the growth rate is maximized when $P=\frac{L}{2}$.
cards.a: Treating $\frac{dP}{dt}$ as a quadratic function of P, $kP-\frac{k}{L}P^{2}$, its graph is a downward parabola whose vertex — the maximum — occurs at $P=-\frac{k}{2\left(-k/L\right)}=\frac{L}{2}$.
cards.h: → dP/dt is a downward parabola in P
cards.n: A second derivative in t also works, but the parabola argument is faster and needs no chain rule at all.

cards.q: For the logistic model $\frac{dP}{dt}=0.03P\left(1-\frac{P}{800}\right)$, compute the maximum possible value of $\frac{dP}{dt}$.
cards.a: 6. The growth rate is fastest at $P=\frac{L}{2}=400$, giving $\frac{dP}{dt}=0.03(400)\left(1-\frac{400}{800}\right)=0.03(400)(0.5)=6$.
cards.n: The maximum RATE occurs at P = L/2, which is different from asking where P itself is largest (P approaches L, not L/2).

cards.q: Contrast the concavity of a logistic solution curve for $0<P(0)<\frac{L}{2}$ versus for $\frac{L}{2}<P(0)<L$.
cards.a: For $0<P<\frac{L}{2}$, the curve is concave up, since the growth rate is still increasing toward its maximum. For $\frac{L}{2}<P<L$, the curve is concave down, since the growth rate is decreasing as P approaches the carrying capacity.
cards.n: Concavity here describes P as a function of t, not the downward parabola that dP/dt traces against P.

cards.q: Verify that $y = 2\sin x - \cos x$ is a solution of y'' + y = 0.
cards.a: Yes. $y'=2\cos x+\sin x$ and $y''=-2\sin x+\cos x$; adding $y''+y = \left(-2\sin x+\cos x\right)+\left(2\sin x-\cos x\right)=0$ for every x.
cards.n: Every combination $a\sin x + b\cos x$ satisfies this equation, which is why both constants stay unrestricted.

cards.q: Decide whether $y = x^{2}$ is a solution of $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x} + 1$.
cards.a: No. y'=2x, but the right side is $\frac{y}{x}+1=\frac{x^{2}}{x}+1=x+1$; these agree only at x=1, not for all x, so $y=x^{2}$ is not a solution.
cards.n: A candidate that satisfies the equation at one x-value is not a solution — the equality must hold identically.

cards.q: For $\frac{dy}{dx} = 2y - x$, find the slope of the segment the slope field draws at the point (1, 3).
cards.a: 5. Substitute the point directly: at (1,3), $\frac{dy}{dx}=2(3)-1=5$.
cards.n: Only the point gets substituted; no solution curve is involved, since the equation reports slopes directly.

cards.q: A slope field has slope 0 on the x-axis, and slopes share the SIGN of y, growing steeper with distance from it. Identify a matching differential equation.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx}=y$. The slope depends only on y, equals 0 exactly on the x-axis (y=0), and its magnitude and sign both track y directly.
cards.n: Identical segments along each horizontal row mean dependence on y alone, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=cy$ with c > 0 fits too.

cards.q: A slope field for $\frac{dy}{dx} = y - 3$ shows curves moving AWAY from the line y=3 on both sides. Decide whether y=3 is a stable or unstable equilibrium, and justify.
cards.a: Unstable. Below y=3, y−3<0 so solutions decrease away from it; above y=3, y−3>0 so solutions increase away from it — nearby solutions move away from y=3 in both directions.
cards.n: Compare to a stable equilibrium: there, both sides move TOWARD the line instead.

cards.q: For $\frac{dy}{dx} = x - y$, a solution curve passes through (0, 0). Describe what happens to its slope as the curve crosses the line y = x.
cards.a: The slope equals 0 exactly when the curve touches the line y = x, since $\frac{dy}{dx}=x-y=0$ there. Above that line (y>x) the slope is negative; below it (y<x) the slope is positive.
cards.h: → set dy/dx = 0 to find where slopes flatten
cards.n: Because the slope is zero exactly on y = x, a solution curve touches that line rather than cutting across it.

cards.q: Write a differential equation modeling: medication A(t) is added at a constant rate of 5 mg per hour, while it is eliminated at a rate proportional to the amount present.
cards.a: $\frac{dA}{dt} = 5 - kA$ for some positive constant k. The constant input rate and the proportional elimination rate combine additively.
cards.n: This is the same algebraic structure as the logistic equation's cousin — a constant term plus a linear term in the unknown.

cards.q: A bacteria culture grows continuously at 8% per hour. If there are 500 bacteria at t=0, compute the population after 6 hours.
cards.n: A stated percentage growth rate per unit time IS the constant k in $\frac{dy}{dt}=ky$, already in decimal form.

cards.q: State the formula for the average value of f on [a, b].
cards.a: $f_{avg} = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$.
cards.n: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{b-a}$ factor is the most common average-value error.

cards.q: Contrast the average VALUE of f with the average RATE OF CHANGE of f on [a, b].
cards.a: Average value is $\frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ (an integral). Average rate of change is $\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$ (a difference quotient, i.e. the average value of f').
cards.n: If the given function is a RATE, its average value is still the integral formula.

cards.q: State the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals.
cards.a: If f is continuous on [a, b], there exists c in (a, b) with $f(c) = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx$ — the function attains its average value somewhere.
cards.n: Continuity on the closed interval is the hypothesis to state before claiming that such a c exists.

cards.q: State the Net Change Theorem for position.
cards.a: $s(b) = s(a) + \int_{a}^{b} v(t)\,dt$: final position equals initial position plus displacement.
cards.n: This integral gives displacement only, so a question about how far the particle traveled needs |v(t)| instead.

cards.q: Define displacement over [a, b] and give its integral.
cards.a: The signed net change in position: $\int_{a}^{b} v(t)\,dt$. It can be negative or zero.
cards.n: Displacement equals total distance only when v keeps a single sign across the whole interval.

cards.q: Define total distance traveled over [a, b] and give its integral.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} |v(t)|\,dt$ — always nonnegative. By hand, split at the times where v changes sign and add the absolute values of the pieces.
cards.n: On the calculator section you may enter the absolute value directly.

cards.q: Contrast displacement with total distance traveled.
cards.a: Displacement is net signed change, $\int v\,dt$; total distance is $\int |v|\,dt$. They agree only when v never changes sign on the interval.
cards.n: 'How far did it travel' means distance; 'how far from the start' means displacement.

cards.q: Explain how to find the total distance a particle travels when v(t) changes sign at t = c inside [a, b].
cards.a: Compute $\left|\int_{a}^{c} v\,dt\right| + \left|\int_{c}^{b} v\,dt\right|$; equivalently $\int_{a}^{b} |v(t)|\,dt$.
cards.n: Find the sign changes first by solving v(t) = 0.

cards.q: Explain how to determine the units of $\int_{a}^{b} R(t)\,dt$.
cards.a: Multiply the units of R by the units of t: if R is gallons per hour and t is hours, the integral is in gallons.
cards.n: Interpretation questions require units plus a context sentence for full credit.

cards.q: Set up the amount remaining at time T when material enters at rate I(t) and leaves at rate O(t), starting from $A_{0}$.
cards.a: $A(T) = A_{0} + \int_{0}^{T} \left( I(t) - O(t) \right)\,dt$.
cards.n: 'In minus out' tank problems appear on nearly every free-response set.

cards.q: Explain how to find when the amount in an in/out rate problem is at a MAXIMUM.
cards.a: Set the net rate I(t) - O(t) = 0, then check that it changes from positive to negative there; compare candidate values including the endpoints.
cards.h: → critical point of the net rate
cards.n: The maximum is where the rate changes sign, not where the rate is largest.

cards.q: State the area between two curves as functions of x.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)\,dx$, where f is the upper curve on [a, b] and a, b are the x-coordinates of the intersections.
cards.n: Vertical rectangles: height is top minus bottom, width is dx.

cards.q: Explain how to decide which function is 'on top' in an area problem.
cards.a: Test a sample x strictly between the intersection points and compare the two outputs; whichever is greater is the top function on that subinterval.
cards.n: Subtracting in the wrong order gives a negative area — a giveaway that you flipped it.

cards.q: State the area between two curves as functions of y.
cards.a: $\int_{c}^{d} \left( f(y) - g(y) \right)\,dy$, where f is the RIGHT curve and g is the LEFT curve, and c, d are the y-coordinates of the intersections.
cards.n: Horizontal rectangles: length is right minus left, thickness is dy.

cards.q: State when integrating with respect to y is easier for an area problem.
cards.a: When the region's left and right boundaries are single curves but the top or bottom boundary switches, or when the curves are naturally written as x = f(y).
cards.n: Choosing dy can turn three integrals into one.

cards.q: Name the setup trap involving dx versus dy.
cards.a: Mixing them: using x-bounds with a dy integral, or leaving a function of x inside a dy integral. Everything inside the integral must be in the same variable as the differential.
cards.n: Check the bounds: dx bounds are x-values, dy bounds are y-values.

cards.q: Explain how to find the area of a region whose boundary curves intersect at MORE than two points.
cards.a: Find all intersections, split the interval at each one, determine which function is on top on each piece with a test point, and add the separate integrals (each written top minus bottom).
cards.n: A single integral with absolute value also works on the calculator section.

cards.q: Explain why $\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)\,dx$ can understate the AREA when the curves cross inside [a, b].
cards.a: Past the crossing the integrand turns negative, so that piece cancels part of the earlier piece. Area needs $\int_{a}^{b} |f(x) - g(x)|\,dx$.
cards.n: Locate every crossing inside [a, b] before writing anything down; a setup that misses one is wrong from the start.

cards.q: State the general volume formula for a solid with known cross sections.
cards.a: $V = \int_{a}^{b} A(x)\,dx$, where A(x) is the area of the cross section at x. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis integrate with dx; perpendicular to the y-axis, dy.
cards.n: Nothing is being revolved, so no pi appears unless the cross section is itself a circle or semicircle.

cards.q: Give the volume integral when cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are SQUARES with base in the region between f and g.
cards.a: $V = \int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$ — the side length is the vertical distance between the curves.
cards.n: No $\pi$ appears; cross-section solids are not solids of revolution.

cards.q: Give the volume integral when cross sections are RECTANGLES of height twice the base.
cards.a: $V = \int_{a}^{b} 2\left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$: area = base times height = s times 2s.
cards.n: Read the stated height ratio carefully; it varies problem to problem.

cards.q: Give the cross-sectional area of an EQUILATERAL TRIANGLE with side s, and the resulting volume integral.
cards.a: $A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}s^{2}$, so $V = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$.
cards.n: The $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ comes from a height of $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s$, and s here is the full vertical gap between the curves.

cards.q: Give the cross-sectional area of a SEMICIRCLE whose DIAMETER is s, and the resulting volume integral.
cards.a: $A = \frac{\pi}{8}s^{2}$ (radius is $\frac{s}{2}$), so $V = \frac{\pi}{8}\int_{a}^{b} \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$.
cards.n: Check whether the problem gives the diameter or the radius; using s as the radius multiplies the answer by 4.

cards.q: Give the cross-sectional area of an ISOSCELES RIGHT TRIANGLE with the LEG on the base, versus the HYPOTENUSE on the base.
cards.a: Leg on the base: $A = \frac{1}{2}s^{2}$. Hypotenuse on the base: $A = \frac{1}{4}s^{2}$.
cards.n: The wording 'leg' versus 'hypotenuse' changes the answer by a factor of 2.

cards.q: State the disc method for revolving a region about the x-axis.
cards.a: $V = \pi\int_{a}^{b} \left( R(x) \right)^{2}\,dx$, where R(x) is the distance from the axis to the curve. Use it when the region touches the axis of revolution.
cards.h: → pi times integral of radius squared
cards.n: The square sits inside the integral, so squaring the finished integral instead gives a completely different number.

cards.q: State the disc method for revolving about the y-axis.
cards.a: $V = \pi\int_{c}^{d} \left( R(y) \right)^{2}\,dy$, with the curve solved for x in terms of y and the bounds as y-values.
cards.n: The bounds must be y-values, so convert any given x-limits by running them through the curve before integrating.

cards.q: Explain how to write the radius when revolving about a horizontal line y = c instead of the x-axis.
cards.a: The radius is the distance from the line to the curve: R(x) = |f(x) − c|. Above the line use f(x) - c; below it use c - f(x).
cards.n: Subtracting the axis value is the whole trick; the rest of the setup is unchanged.

cards.q: Explain how to write the radius when revolving about a vertical line x = k.
cards.a: R(y) = |x(y) − k|, the horizontal distance from the line to the curve, and integrate with respect to y.
cards.n: Sketch the region first to see which side of x = k it lies on, then drop the bars by writing larger minus smaller.

cards.q: State the washer method.
cards.a: $V = \pi\int_{a}^{b} \left( \left( R(x) \right)^{2} - \left( r(x) \right)^{2} \right)\,dx$, where R is the outer radius and r the inner radius. Use it when a gap separates the region from the axis.
cards.h: → pi times integral of R squared minus r squared
cards.n: The difference of squares cannot be collapsed into $\left(R-r\right)^{2}$, which is a different and smaller quantity.

cards.q: Name the algebra trap in the washer method.
cards.a: Writing $\left( R - r \right)^{2}$ instead of $R^{2} - r^{2}$. You subtract the AREAS of the two circles, not the radii.
cards.n: This error is worth several points and is easy to miss in a rush.

cards.q: Explain how to set up a washer volume about a horizontal line y = c below the region.
cards.a: Outer radius R = (far curve) - c and inner radius r = (near curve) - c, then $V = \pi\int_{a}^{b} \left( R^{2} - r^{2} \right)\,dx$. Identify which curve is farther from the axis, not which is on top.
cards.n: When the axis lies above the region, the roles of the curves swap.

cards.q: State the shell (cylindrical shells) method for revolving about the y-axis.
cards.a: $V = 2\pi\int_{a}^{b} x \cdot \left( f(x) - g(x) \right)\,dx$ — radius times height times thickness. About a vertical line x = k, the radius becomes |x - k|.
cards.h: → two-pi times integral of radius times height
cards.n: Shells are NOT required by the AP CED; discs and washers suffice, but shells can be faster.

cards.q: State when the shell method is more convenient than washers.
cards.a: When the region is easy to describe in x but is revolved about a VERTICAL axis (or vice versa), so shells avoid solving the curves for the other variable.
cards.n: Shells are not on the AP CED, so every exam volume can be finished with discs or washers if you prefer.

cards.q: State the arc length formula for y = f(x) on [a, b].
cards.a: $L = \int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1 + \left( f'(x) \right)^{2}}\,dx$, valid when f' is continuous on [a, b].
cards.n: BC only; on the exam this is almost always evaluated with the calculator.

cards.q: State the arc length formula for a curve written as x = g(y) on [c, d].
cards.a: $L = \int_{c}^{d}\sqrt{1 + \left( g'(y) \right)^{2}}\,dy$.
cards.n: Reach for this form when the curve has a vertical tangent, where dy/dx blows up but dx/dy stays finite.

cards.q: Set up the arc length of $y = x^{2}$ from x = 0 to x = 3.
cards.n: On the calculator section, write the integral first, then report the numeric value to three decimals.

cards.q: State what must appear on the page when a calculator evaluates an integral on the free-response.
cards.a: The SETUP: the definite integral with correct integrand and limits, then the numerical answer. A bare number with no integral shown earns almost no credit.
cards.n: Write the integral even when you solve entirely on the calculator.

cards.q: Explain why you should store intermediate values in the calculator rather than rewriting them.
cards.a: Storing keeps full precision. Re-entering a value rounded to three decimals propagates error, and a later answer can fall outside the scoring tolerance.
cards.n: Scoring allows three decimal places, so carry extra digits through every step and round only the reported answer.

cards.q: State the convention for leaving answers unsimplified on AP Calculus free-response.
cards.a: Numerical answers need not be simplified; an unsimplified exact expression is fine. On calculator problems give a decimal to three or more places. Do not round until the final step.
cards.n: Time spent simplifying earns no points.

cards.q: Name the most common wrong-function error in area and volume setups.
cards.a: Subtracting bottom minus top (or left minus right), which flips the sign, and using the WRONG pair of curves after a crossing point. Always test a point in each subinterval.
cards.n: A negative area or volume is the tell; if the arithmetic returns one, the two curves were subtracted backwards.

cards.q: Explain how to find the bounds of integration for a volume problem when they are not given.
cards.a: Solve for the intersections of the boundary curves (or the intercepts if one boundary is an axis); those coordinates are the limits, in x for dx setups and in y for dy setups.
cards.n: Set the boundary curves equal and solve, and on the calculator section store the intersection instead of rounding it.

cards.q: Find the arc length of $y=\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2}$ from x=0 to x=3.
cards.n: This is one of the rare arc length integrands that simplifies exactly; most of them need the calculator.

cards.q: Find the volume when the region under $y=\sqrt{x}$ on [0,4] is revolved about the x-axis.
cards.a: $8\pi$. $V=\pi\int_{0}^{4} \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}\,dx = \pi\int_{0}^{4} x\,dx = \pi\left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{4} = 8\pi$.
cards.n: Squaring the radius clears the root, which is why this one is exact by hand while most volume integrals are not.

cards.q: Find the volume when the region bounded by $y=x^{2}$, y=4 (for $x \ge 0$) is revolved about the y-axis.
cards.a: $8\pi$. Rewrite as $x=\sqrt{y}$: $V=\pi\int_{0}^{4}\left(\sqrt{y}\right)^{2}\,dy=\pi\int_{0}^{4} y\,dy=8\pi$.
cards.n: Revolving about the y-axis forces dy, so solve for x first; integrating in x would answer a different question.

cards.q: Find the volume when the region between $y=x^{2}$ and y=x (for $0\le x\le1$) is revolved about the x-axis.
cards.a: $\frac{2\pi}{15}$. Outer radius x, inner radius $x^{2}$: $V=\pi\int_{0}^{1}\left(x^{2}-x^{4}\right)\,dx=\pi\left(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{5}\right)=\frac{2\pi}{15}$.
cards.n: Since x ≥ x² on [0,1], the line is the OUTER radius, not the parabola — check with a test point like x=1/2.

cards.q: Find the volume when the region under $y=x^{2}$ on [0,2] is revolved about the line x=−1, using shells.
cards.a: $\frac{40\pi}{3}$. Shell radius is x+1, height is $x^{2}$: $V=2\pi\int_{0}^{2}(x+1)x^{2}\,dx=2\pi\left[\frac{x^{4}}{4}+\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}=2\pi\left(4+\frac{8}{3}\right)=\frac{40\pi}{3}$.
cards.n: Shifting the axis to x=-1 adds 1 to the radius everywhere; forgetting the shift is the most common error.

cards.q: Find the average value of $f(x)=x^{2}$ on [0,3].
cards.a: 3. Average value $=\frac{1}{3}\int_{0}^{3} x^{2}\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\left(9\right) = 3$.
cards.n: Average value is a height rather than an area, so dividing by the width b - a is the step you cannot skip.

cards.q: Find the average value of $f(x)=\sin x$ on $[0,\pi]$.
cards.a: $\frac{2}{\pi}$. Average value $=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=\frac{1}{\pi}\left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi}=\frac{1}{\pi}(1-(-1))=\frac{2}{\pi}$.
cards.n: About 0.64, comfortably below the peak value 1, which is the sanity check every average value must pass.

cards.q: A particle has velocity $v(t)=3t^{2}-6t$ and s(0)=4. Find its position at t=3.
cards.n: The particle returns to its starting position even though it moved during the interval — net displacement is 0.

cards.q: A particle has $v(t)=t^{2}-4$ for $0\le t\le3$. Find the total distance traveled.
cards.a: 23/3. Split at t=2 where v changes sign: $\int_{0}^{2}(4-t^{2})\,dt=\frac{16}{3}$ plus $\int_{2}^{3}(t^{2}-4)\,dt=\frac{7}{3}$.
cards.n: Solve v(t) = 0 inside the interval first; the absolute value cannot be integrated by hand without that split.

cards.q: Find the area between $y=x^{2}$ and y=2x on the interval where they overlap.
cards.a: 4/3. The curves meet at x=0 and x=2, with $2x \ge x^{2}$ between them: $\int_{0}^{2}\left(2x-x^{2}\right)\,dx = \left[x^{2}-\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}=4-\frac{8}{3}=\frac{4}{3}$.
cards.n: The phrase where they overlap is the only source of the bounds, so setting the curves equal comes first.

cards.q: The base is the region between $y=x^{2}$ and y=4 (for $-2\le x\le2$); cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. Find the volume.
cards.a: $\frac{512}{15}$. Side length $4-x^{2}$ gives area $\left(4-x^{2}\right)^{2}$; by symmetry $V=2\int_{0}^{2}\left(16-8x^{2}+x^{4}\right)\,dx = \frac{512}{15}$.
cards.n: Using symmetry is optional but halves the algebra, and it is legitimate only because the integrand is even in x.

cards.q: The base is bounded by $y=\sqrt{x}$, the x-axis, and x=4; cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are semicircles with diameter from the axis to the curve. Find the volume.
cards.a: $\pi$. Diameter $\sqrt{x}$ gives radius $\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2}$ and semicircle area $\frac{\pi x}{8}$: $V=\int_{0}^{4}\frac{\pi x}{8}\,dx=\pi$.
cards.n: The segment from the axis to the curve is the DIAMETER, so halving it before squaring is the whole trap here.

cards.q: Find the area between $y=\sin x$ and the x-axis on $[0,2\pi]$.
cards.a: 4. Split at x=π where sin x changes sign: $\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx=2$ and $\int_{\pi}^{2\pi}\left(-\sin x\right)\,dx=2$, for a total of 4.
cards.n: A single integral of $|\sin x|$ over the full interval gives the same 4 without splitting by hand.

cards.q: Find the average value of $f(x)=3x^{2}-2$ on [0,2].
cards.a: 2. The average value is $\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{2}\left(3x^{2}-2\right)dx=\frac{1}{2}\left[x^{3}-2x\right]_{0}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(8-4)=2$.
cards.n: The result has to land between the minimum and maximum of f on the interval, which is the quickest check.

cards.q: A particle moves with velocity $v(t)=\sin(\pi t)+2$ and s(0)=3. Find its position at t=2.
cards.a: s(2)=7. An antiderivative is $s(t)=-\frac{1}{\pi}\cos(\pi t)+2t+C$; using s(0)=3 gives $C=3+\frac{1}{\pi}$, so $s(2)=-\frac{1}{\pi}+4+3+\frac{1}{\pi}=7$.
cards.n: The cosine terms cancel because the interval spans a whole period, so the sine wave contributes nothing net.

cards.q: A particle has $v(t)=t^{2}-2t-3$ on [0,4] with s(0)=0. Compute both the displacement and the total distance traveled.
cards.a: Displacement is $-\frac{20}{3}$; total distance is $\frac{34}{3}$. Since v changes sign at t=3, displacement integrates v directly over [0,4], while total distance requires splitting at t=3 and integrating |v| on each piece.
cards.n: These two answers differ specifically because the particle reverses direction partway through the interval — check for sign changes in v before assuming they're equal.

cards.q: Water enters a tank at rate $I(t)=5\sqrt{t}$ gal/min and leaves at rate O(t)=3 gal/min for $0 \le t \le 9$. If the tank has 20 gallons at t=0, compute the amount at t=9.
cards.a: 83 gallons. The net change is $\int_{0}^{9}\left(5\sqrt{t}-3\right)dt=\left[\frac{10}{3}t^{3/2}-3t\right]_{0}^{9}=90-27=63$, so the total is 20+63=83.
cards.n: Subtract the outflow inside the integral rather than afterwards, and add the initial 20 gallons at the end.

cards.q: Find the area of the region bounded by $x=y^{2}$ and x=4, integrating with respect to y.
cards.a: $\frac{32}{3}$. The curves meet at $y=\pm2$, so the area is $\int_{-2}^{2}\left(4-y^{2}\right)dy=\left[4y-\frac{y^{3}}{3}\right]_{-2}^{2}=\frac{32}{3}$.
cards.h: → right boundary minus left boundary, in y
cards.n: An x-setup would need the top half doubled, so integrating in y avoids splitting the region at all.

cards.q: Find the area of the region bounded by x=y+2 and $x=y^{2}$, integrating with respect to y.
cards.a: $\frac{9}{2}$. The curves meet at y=-1 and y=2, so the area is $\int_{-1}^{2}\left[(y+2)-y^{2}\right]dy=\frac{9}{2}$.
cards.n: Setting up the correct 'right minus left' boundary in y is easy to get backwards — sketch the region first.

cards.q: Find the area between $y=x^{3}$ and y=x on [−1,1].
cards.a: $\frac{1}{2}$. The curves cross at x=-1, 0, 1; by symmetry, the area is $2\int_{0}^{1}\left(x-x^{3}\right)dx=2\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{1}{2}$.
cards.n: The curves swap which one is on top between (-1,0) and (0,1) — a single integral of $(x^{3}-x)$ across the whole interval would give the wrong, cancelled-out answer.

cards.q: The base of a solid is bounded by $y=\sin x$ and the x-axis on $[0,\pi]$; cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are squares. Find the volume.
cards.a: $\frac{\pi}{2}$. The volume is $\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin^{2}x\,dx$, and using the power-reduction identity this evaluates to $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
cards.n: The power-reduction identity is required because $\sin^{2}x$ has no antiderivative in the formula list.

cards.q: The base of a solid is bounded by $y=4-x^{2}$ and the x-axis; cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are equilateral triangles. Find the volume.
cards.a: $\frac{128\sqrt{3}}{15}$. Each side has length $4-x^{2}$, so the volume is $\int_{-2}^{2}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\left(4-x^{2}\right)^{2}dx=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\cdot\frac{512}{15}=\frac{128\sqrt{3}}{15}$.
cards.n: The bounds come from the x-intercepts of $4-x^{2}$, and the constant $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$ belongs outside the integral.

cards.q: Find the volume when the region bounded by y=3−x and the coordinate axes in the first quadrant is revolved about the x-axis.
cards.a: $9\pi$. Using discs, $V=\pi\int_{0}^{3}\left(3-x\right)^{2}dx=\pi\left[-\frac{(3-x)^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{3}=\pi(9)=9\pi$.
cards.n: Revolving about an axis that IS one of the boundaries still uses discs, not washers, since the inner radius is 0.

cards.q: The region bounded by $y=x^{2}$ and y=4 is revolved about the line y=6. Compute the volume using washers.
cards.a: $\frac{384\pi}{5}$. The outer radius is $6-x^{2}$ and the inner radius is 6−4=2, so $V=\pi\int_{-2}^{2}\left[\left(6-x^{2}\right)^{2}-4\right]dx=\frac{384\pi}{5}$.
cards.n: Revolving about a line ABOVE the region still uses washers — do not assume 'above' means discs.

cards.q: The region bounded by $y=\sqrt{x}$ and y=0 on [0,4] is revolved about the line y=−1. Compute the volume using washers.
cards.a: $\frac{56\pi}{3}$. The outer radius is $\sqrt{x}+1$ and the inner radius is 1, so $V=\pi\int_{0}^{4}\left[\left(\sqrt{x}+1\right)^{2}-1\right]dx=\frac{56\pi}{3}$.
cards.n: Moving the axis down adds 1 to every radius, so the inner radius is 1 instead of 0 and washers replace discs.

cards.q: The region bounded by $y=x^{2}$ and y=1 is revolved about the line y=3. Compute the volume using washers.
cards.a: $\frac{32\pi}{5}$. The outer radius is $3-x^{2}$ (from the farther parabola) and the inner radius is 3−1=2 (from the line y=1), so $V=\pi\int_{-1}^{1}\left[\left(3-x^{2}\right)^{2}-4\right]dx=\frac{32\pi}{5}$.
cards.h: → outer radius from the curve farther from the axis
cards.n: Both radii are measured downward from y = 3, so swapping outer and inner would flip the sign of the volume.

cards.q: The region bounded by $x=y^{2}$ and x=4 is revolved about the line x=4. Compute the volume using the disc method.
cards.a: $\frac{512\pi}{15}$. Since x=4 IS the axis of revolution, each cross section is a full disc with radius $R(y)=4-y^{2}$ (no inner hole): $V=\pi\int_{-2}^{2}\left(4-y^{2}\right)^{2}dy=\frac{512\pi}{15}$.
cards.n: Because the axis IS one of the region's own boundaries, there is no inner radius to subtract — this stays a disc problem, not a washer.

cards.q: Find the volume when the region between $y=4-x^{2}$ and y=1 is revolved about the x-axis.
cards.a: $\frac{88\sqrt{3}}{5}\pi$. The curves meet at $x=\pm\sqrt{3}$; outer radius $4-x^{2}$, inner radius 1: $V=\pi\int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}\left[\left(4-x^{2}\right)^{2}-1\right]dx = \frac{88\sqrt{3}}{5}\pi$.
cards.n: Check which boundary is farther from the axis with a test point before assigning outer vs inner radius — here $4-x^{2} \ge 1$ throughout.

cards.q: Define a parametric curve in the plane.
cards.a: A pair of functions x = x(t) and y = y(t) on an interval of t. Each value of the parameter t gives one point (x(t), y(t)); as t increases the point traces the curve in a definite direction.
cards.n: The parameter usually means time on the AP exam, so direction of motion is part of the answer.

cards.q: State the formula for the slope of a parametric curve.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}$, valid wherever $\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0$.
cards.n: Chain rule in disguise: dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt). The t's cancel, not the d's.

cards.q: For $x = t^{2} + 1$ and $y = t^{3} - 3t$, compute $\frac{dy}{dx}$ in terms of t.
cards.n: Leave the answer in terms of t; converting to x is almost never required.

cards.q: Identify the condition for a parametric curve to have a horizontal tangent.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$ while $\frac{dx}{dt} \ne 0$ at that value of t.
cards.n: Both conditions must be stated; a point where both vanish is not automatically horizontal.

cards.q: Identify the condition for a parametric curve to have a vertical tangent.
cards.a: $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ while $\frac{dy}{dt} \ne 0$ at that value of t.
cards.n: Vertical tangents are invisible to dy/dx; find them by setting the denominator to zero.

cards.q: Explain what happens at a value of t where $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$ and $\frac{dy}{dt} = 0$ simultaneously.
cards.a: The particle is instantaneously at rest and dy/dx is undefined there. The curve may have a cusp, a corner, or a smooth point; you cannot decide from the first derivatives alone.
cards.n: Cusps on curves like the cycloid occur exactly at these singular parameter values.

cards.q: Describe how to eliminate the parameter from x = 2t, $y = t^{2} - 1$.
cards.a: Solve one equation for t and substitute: t = x/2, so $y = \frac{x^{2}}{4} - 1$, a parabola.
cards.n: Eliminating the parameter can lose the domain and the direction of travel; state any restriction.

cards.q: State the formula for the second derivative of a parametric curve.
cards.a: $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{d(dy/dx)/dt}{dx/dt}$: differentiate $\frac{dy}{dx}$ with respect to t, then divide by $\frac{dx}{dt}$.
cards.n: It is the first-derivative rule applied to the function dy/dx, not to y.

cards.q: Explain why $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ is not $\frac{d^{2}y/dt^{2}}{d^{2}x/dt^{2}}$.
cards.a: The slope rule applies to a first derivative of a quantity with respect to t. The second derivative is the t-rate of change of dy/dx divided by dx/dt; second t-derivatives of x and y never appear as a ratio.
cards.h: → name the correct chain of steps
cards.n: This is the single most common parametric error on the free-response section.

cards.q: For $x = t^{2}$ and $y = t^{3}$ (t > 0), compute $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^{2}}{2t} = \frac{3t}{2}$; its t-derivative is $\frac{3}{2}$; divide by $\frac{dx}{dt} = 2t$ to get $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} = \frac{3}{4t}$.
cards.h: → three-step chain to an expression in t
cards.n: Simplify dy/dx before differentiating; it saves a quotient rule.

cards.q: Explain how to determine where a parametric curve is concave up.
cards.a: Compute $\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$ as a function of t and find the t-intervals where it is positive; those parameter values give the concave-up portions of the curve.
cards.n: Report the answer in terms of t unless the question explicitly asks for x-values.

cards.q: State the arc length of a parametric curve on $a \le t \le b$.
cards.a: $L = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^{2}}\, dt$.
cards.h: → integral of a square root of squares
cards.n: Same integrand as speed; length is the accumulated speed over the time interval.

cards.q: State the arc length of the graph of y = f(x) from x = a to x = b.
cards.a: $L = \int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}\, dx$.
cards.n: It is the parametric formula with x = t, so dx/dt = 1 produces the leading 1.

cards.q: Set up the arc length of $x = \cos t$, $y = t^{2}$ for $0 \le t \le 2$.
cards.a: $L = \int_{0}^{2} \sqrt{\sin^{2} t + 4t^{2}}\, dt$ (evaluate with a calculator).
cards.n: On calculator-active problems, set up correctly and let the calculator finish; the setup carries the points.

cards.q: Contrast arc length of a parametric curve with the distance a particle travels along it.
cards.a: Both use $\int \sqrt{(dx/dt)^{2} + (dy/dt)^{2}}\, dt$, but arc length measures the curve once, while distance traveled counts every retraced pass. If the parametrization repeats a portion, distance exceeds length.
cards.n: A cardioid traced twice has distance equal to twice its arc length.

cards.q: Define a vector-valued function of a real variable t.
cards.a: A function that assigns to each t a vector, written r(t) = <x(t), y(t)>. Its components are ordinary real-valued functions, and limits, derivatives, and integrals are taken componentwise.
cards.n: Angle-bracket notation and parametric notation carry identical information on the AP exam.

cards.q: State the derivative of the vector-valued function r(t) = <x(t), y(t)>.
cards.a: r'(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)>: differentiate each component separately.
cards.n: Every derivative rule you know applies to each component independently.

cards.q: Define the velocity vector of a particle whose position is <x(t), y(t)>.
cards.a: v(t) = <x'(t), y'(t)>. Its direction is the direction of motion and it is tangent to the path.
cards.n: Velocity is a vector; speed is a number. Confusing them costs points.

cards.q: Define the acceleration vector of a particle whose position is <x(t), y(t)>.
cards.a: a(t) = <x''(t), y''(t)>, the componentwise derivative of the velocity vector.
cards.n: Acceleration is not the derivative of speed; that scalar is the rate of change of speed.

cards.q: State the speed of a particle moving with velocity <x'(t), y'(t)>.
cards.a: speed $= \sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y'(t)\right)^{2}}$, the magnitude of the velocity vector.
cards.n: Speed is never negative and is zero exactly when both velocity components vanish.

cards.q: A particle has x'(t) = 3t and y'(t) = 4t. Compute its speed at t = 2.
cards.n: Substitute t first, then take the magnitude; do not simplify symbolically unless asked.

cards.q: Identify how to tell when a particle in the plane is at rest.
cards.a: Both velocity components are zero at the same t: x'(t) = 0 and y'(t) = 0, so the speed is 0.
cards.n: One component being zero only means motion is momentarily horizontal or vertical.

cards.q: Explain how to find the rate of change of speed at time t.
cards.a: Differentiate the speed function $\sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y'(t)\right)^{2}}$ with respect to t, or evaluate it numerically on a calculator. Its sign tells whether the particle is speeding up or slowing down.
cards.n: AP asks 'is the speed increasing at t = c?' Answer with the sign of the derivative of speed, not of acceleration.

cards.q: State how to recover position from velocity for a particle in the plane.
cards.a: Integrate componentwise and use the initial condition: $x(b) = x(a) + \int_{a}^{b} x'(t)\, dt$ and $y(b) = y(a) + \int_{a}^{b} y'(t)\, dt$.
cards.n: Omitting the initial position is the classic slip; the integral alone gives only displacement.

cards.q: A particle has velocity <cos t, 2t> and position (3, 1) at t = 0. Find its position at t = 2.
cards.n: Do the two components as separate accumulation-function problems.

cards.q: Define the displacement vector of a particle over $a \le t \le b$.
cards.a: The vector whose components are $\int_{a}^{b} x'(t)\, dt$ and $\int_{a}^{b} y'(t)\, dt$, equivalently <x(b) - x(a), y(b) - y(a)>: the straight-line change in position.
cards.n: Displacement can be the zero vector even when the particle travels a long distance.

cards.q: State the total distance traveled by a particle in the plane on $a \le t \le b$.
cards.a: $\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{\left(x'(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y'(t)\right)^{2}}\, dt$, the integral of the speed.
cards.n: No absolute value bars are needed; the square root is already nonnegative.

cards.q: Contrast displacement and total distance for a particle moving in the plane.
cards.a: Displacement is the vector <x(b) - x(a), y(b) - y(a)> and can be zero. Total distance is $\int_{a}^{b} \sqrt{(x')^{2} + (y')^{2}}\, dt$, a nonnegative scalar equal to the path length traveled.
cards.n: Read the verb: 'how far from the start' is displacement, 'how far did it travel' is distance.

cards.q: Explain how to decide whether a particle in the plane is speeding up at time t.
cards.a: The particle speeds up when the dot product of velocity and acceleration is positive, equivalently when the derivative of the speed function is positive at that t.
cards.n: In one dimension this reduces to v and a having the same sign.

cards.q: Write the equation of the tangent line to a parametric curve at the point where t = c.
cards.a: Compute the point (x(c), y(c)) and the slope $m = \frac{y'(c)}{x'(c)}$, then use $y - y(c) = m\left(x - x(c)\right)$.
cards.n: The slope must be evaluated at t = c, not left as a function of t.

cards.q: Explain how to find when a particle moving in the plane is farthest from the origin on a closed t-interval.
cards.a: Maximize $D(t) = \sqrt{\left(x(t)\right)^{2} + \left(y(t)\right)^{2}}$ by checking critical values of D (or of D squared) together with the interval endpoints.
cards.n: Maximizing the square of the distance avoids the square root and gives the same location.

cards.q: State the conversions from polar coordinates to rectangular coordinates.
cards.a: $x = r \cos \theta$ and $y = r \sin \theta$.
cards.n: These make every polar curve a parametric curve with parameter theta.

cards.q: State the conversions from rectangular coordinates to polar coordinates.
cards.a: $r^{2} = x^{2} + y^{2}$ and $\tan \theta = \frac{y}{x}$ (choose theta in the correct quadrant).
cards.n: The arctangent alone lands in quadrant I or IV; adjust by pi for points on the left half-plane.

cards.q: State the formula for $\frac{dy}{dx}$ for a polar curve $r = f(\theta)$.
cards.a: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}$ where $x = f(\theta) \cos \theta$ and $y = f(\theta) \sin \theta$; each numerator and denominator needs the product rule.
cards.h: → parametric slope with theta as parameter
cards.n: dy/dx is never $\frac{dr}{d\theta}$; that quantity is only how fast the radius changes.

cards.q: For $r = 1 + \cos \theta$, write $\frac{dy}{d\theta}$.
cards.a: $y = \left(1 + \cos \theta\right) \sin \theta$, so $\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -\sin^{2} \theta + \left(1 + \cos \theta\right) \cos \theta$.
cards.n: Build y first, then differentiate; trying to shortcut with $\frac{dr}{d\theta}$ gives a wrong slope.

cards.q: Explain the meaning of a negative value of r in polar coordinates.
cards.a: The point is plotted a distance |r| from the pole in the direction opposite theta, that is at angle $\theta + \pi$.
cards.n: Negative r lets a rose or limacon trace petals in unexpected quadrants.

cards.q: Identify why a single point has infinitely many polar representations.
cards.a: Adding any multiple of $2\pi$ to theta names the same point, and the pair $(-r, \theta + \pi)$ also names it; the pole itself is (0, theta) for every theta.
cards.n: This is exactly why solving two polar equations can miss an intersection.

cards.q: Explain what $\frac{dr}{d\theta} > 0$ tells you about a polar curve.
cards.a: The distance from the pole is increasing as theta increases: the curve is moving away from the origin. It says nothing directly about the slope of the tangent line.
cards.n: AP asks this to test whether students confuse $\frac{dr}{d\theta}$ with dy/dx.

cards.q: State the area enclosed by the polar curve $r = f(\theta)$ between the rays theta = a and theta = b.
cards.a: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{a}^{b} r^{2}\, d\theta$, where the curve is traced exactly once from a to b.
cards.n: Forgetting the one-half or forgetting to square r are the two most common polar-area errors.

cards.q: Explain where the factor $\frac{1}{2}r^{2}$ in the polar area formula comes from.
cards.a: A thin wedge of angle $d\theta$ at radius r is nearly a circular sector, whose area is $\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\, d\theta$; summing the sectors gives the integral.
cards.n: Knowing the sector origin makes the missing one-half impossible to forget.

cards.q: Find the theta-limits for one petal of $r = \sin \left(3\theta\right)$.
cards.a: The petal is traced as r goes from 0 up and back to 0: $\sin(3\theta) = 0$ at $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$, so use $0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{3}$.
cards.n: Correct bounds for one petal are consecutive zeros of r, not a full 2 pi sweep.

cards.q: Set up the area of one petal of $r = 2\cos \left(2\theta\right)$.
cards.a: Zeros of r at $\theta = -\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\theta = \frac{\pi}{4}$, so $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} 4\cos^{2}\left(2\theta\right)\, d\theta$.
cards.n: Squaring the 2 outside the cosine is required; (2cos 2t) squared is 4 cos squared 2t.

cards.q: Explain the risk of integrating a polar area from 0 to $2\pi$ without checking the graph.
cards.a: If the curve is traced more than once on that interval, the integral counts the region multiple times and the area is too large. Always integrate over an interval that traces the region exactly once.
cards.n: For r = cos theta the full circle is traced on 0 to pi; integrating to 2 pi doubles the area.

cards.q: State the area of the region between two polar curves with outer radius R(theta) and inner radius r(theta) on a to b.
cards.a: $A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{a}^{b} \left(R^{2} - r^{2}\right)\, d\theta$.
cards.h: → half integral of a difference of squares
cards.n: Subtract the squares, never square the difference: R squared minus r squared, not (R - r) squared.

cards.q: Explain how to find the theta-values where two polar curves intersect.
cards.a: Set the two expressions for r equal and solve for theta, then separately check whether both curves pass through the pole, since the pole can be reached at different theta values on each curve.
cards.h: → solve, then check one special point
cards.n: Simultaneous solving alone misses pole intersections and the (-r, theta + pi) representations.

cards.q: State the general method for setting up the area of a region inside one polar curve and outside another.
cards.a: Identify which curve is farther from the pole on each theta-interval, then integrate $\frac{1}{2}\left(R^{2} - r^{2}\right)$ over that interval, splitting the integral wherever the outer and inner curves switch roles.
cards.n: Sketch first: which curve is outer can change at each intersection angle.

cards.q: Explain how symmetry can shorten a polar area computation.
cards.a: If the region is symmetric about a line, integrate over half of it and double the result, but only after confirming the symmetry from the equation or graph.
cards.h: → halve the interval, double the value
cards.n: Assumed symmetry that is not actually present is a common source of a factor-of-two error.

cards.q: Identify the graph of the polar equation r = a for a constant a > 0.
cards.a: A circle of radius a centered at the pole (origin).
cards.n: The simplest polar graph; theta is unrestricted.

cards.q: Identify the graphs of $r = a \cos \theta$ and $r = a \sin \theta$.
cards.a: Circles of diameter |a| passing through the pole: $r = a \cos \theta$ is centered on the x-axis at (a/2, 0), and $r = a \sin \theta$ is centered on the y-axis at (0, a/2). Each is traced once on an interval of length pi.
cards.n: The 'traced once over pi' fact prevents doubling the area.

cards.q: Name the curve $r = a \pm a \cos \theta$ (or with sine) and describe its shape.
cards.a: A cardioid: a heart-shaped curve that reaches the pole at exactly one theta and has maximum radius 2a.
cards.n: A cardioid is the limacon case where the constant and the coefficient are equal.

cards.q: Contrast the three cases of the limacon $r = a + b\cos \theta$ with a, b > 0.
cards.a: If a < b the limacon has an inner loop; if a = b it is a cardioid; if b < a < 2b it is dimpled; if $a \ge 2b$ it is convex with no dimple.
cards.n: The ratio a/b decides everything; compare it to 1 and to 2.

cards.q: Recall the number of petals of the rose curves $r = a\cos \left(n\theta\right)$ and $r = a\sin \left(n\theta\right)$.
cards.a: If n is odd there are n petals (traced once on 0 to pi); if n is even there are 2n petals (traced once on 0 to 2 pi).
cards.h: → two cases by parity of n
cards.n: Odd n gives n petals, even n gives 2n; getting this wrong ruins both the bounds and the area.

cards.q: Name the curve $r^{2} = a^{2}\sin \left(2\theta\right)$ and describe it.
cards.a: A lemniscate: a two-loop figure-eight through the pole, oriented along the line theta = pi/4 for the sine form (along the x-axis for the cosine form).
cards.n: r squared must be nonnegative, so the curve exists only where sin 2 theta is at least 0.

cards.q: Identify the graph of $r = a\theta$ for $\theta \ge 0$.
cards.a: An Archimedean spiral: the radius grows in direct proportion to the angle, so the curve winds outward with evenly spaced turns.
cards.n: Spirals are never traced once on a bounded interval; area questions must state explicit bounds.

cards.q: Explain how to find the maximum distance from the pole on a polar curve $r = f(\theta)$.
cards.a: Maximize |f(theta)| over the given theta-interval: find where $\frac{dr}{d\theta} = 0$ and compare those values with the interval endpoints.
cards.n: This is the one polar question where $\frac{dr}{d\theta}$, not dy/dx, is the right tool.
