cards.n: Using this test when f''(c) = 0 earns no credit - it is inconclusive by definition.

cards.q: Recall the wording that identifies a point of inflection with justification.
cards.a: f''(x) changes sign at x = c, so the graph of f has a point of inflection at x = c. State the actual sign on each side, for example negative then positive.
cards.h: → f'' changes sign, then name the point of inflection
cards.n: f''(c) = 0 alone is not enough - the sign must actually change on either side of c.

cards.q: Recall the wording that earns an Integral Test justification for a series.
cards.a: Let f(x) match the series terms. f is positive, continuous, and decreasing for x ≥ N, so the series and $\int_N^{∞} f(x) dx$ either both converge or both diverge; evaluate the integral to decide which.
cards.h: → positive, continuous, decreasing + shared convergence behavior
cards.n: All three conditions - positive, continuous, decreasing - must be checked, not assumed.

cards.q: Recall the wording that earns an Alternating Series Test justification.
cards.a: The terms alternate in sign, |a_n| is decreasing, and $\lim_{n→∞} a_n = 0$, so by the Alternating Series Test the series converges.
cards.h: → alternates + decreasing + terms → 0, so it converges
cards.n: All three conditions must be verified - decreasing terms alone, without the limit condition, is incomplete.

cards.q: Recall the wording that earns a Ratio Test justification for radius of convergence.
cards.a: Compute $\lim_{n→∞} |\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}|$. The series converges where this limit is less than 1, so solve that inequality for x to find the radius of convergence.
cards.h: → set up the limit of the ratio, solve limit < 1
cards.n: The ratio test alone never determines what happens at the two endpoints - those need separate tests.

cards.q: Explain what the nth term test can and cannot prove about a series.
cards.a: If the limit of a_n as n → ∞ is not 0, the series diverges. If the limit is 0, the test proves nothing about convergence - some other test must be used.
cards.h: → nonzero limit proves divergence only; zero limit proves nothing
cards.n: Using this test to claim convergence when the limit is 0 is a very common wrong justification.

cards.q: Recall the wording that earns full credit on a Lagrange error bound justification.
cards.a: $|R_n(x)| ≤ M\frac{|x-a|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}$, where M is an upper bound for $|f^{(n+1)}(t)|$ on the interval between a and x. State the value of M you used and where it came from.
cards.h: → state the bound formula, then justify the value of M
cards.n: Plugging in a value for M without saying where it came from usually loses part of the point.

cards.q: A problem gives f with a corner (not smooth) at x = 3 on [1,5]. Explain why the Mean Value Theorem cannot guarantee a c with f'(c) equal to the average rate of change on [1,5].
cards.a: MVT requires f to be differentiable on (1,5). Since f has a corner at x = 3, f is not differentiable there, so the hypothesis fails and MVT does not apply - no such c is guaranteed.
cards.h: → name the hypothesis that fails (differentiability), and why
cards.n: Naming which hypothesis fails, not just saying 'MVT doesn't work here,' is what earns the point.

cards.q: Water flows into a tank at R(t) = 20 + 3sin(t/4) gallons/hour and out at a constant 15 gallons/hour, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 8. The tank holds 40 gallons at t = 0. Find the amount of water at t = 8.
cards.a: Amount = 40 + $\int_0^8 [R(t)-15] dt$. Evaluating (calculator allowed): 40 + 56.994 = 96.994 gallons. Points earned: the correct integral expression with correct bounds, and the evaluated total including the initial 40.
cards.h: → initial amount + ∫(rate in − rate out) dt
cards.n: The most common miss is forgetting to add the initial 40 gallons back to the integral's value.

cards.q: For the tank with R(t) = 20 + 3sin(t/4) in and 15 out, is the amount of water increasing or decreasing at t = 5? Justify.
cards.a: R(5) - 15 = 20 + 3sin(1.25) - 15 ≈ 7.85, which is positive, so the amount of water is increasing at t = 5 because the rate in exceeds the rate out at that instant.
cards.h: → sign of (rate in − rate out) at t=5, then a sentence
cards.n: The justification must compare rate in to rate out by name, not just report a positive number.

cards.q: For the same tank, find the time t in [0,8] when the amount of water is at a minimum, and justify that it is a minimum.
cards.a: Solve R(t) = 15 to find the critical time(s). Use the first derivative test on the amount function - it decreases while rate in < rate out and increases after - or compare candidate values including t = 0 and t = 8 to confirm the minimum.
cards.h: → solve rate in = rate out, then justify with a sign change or candidates test
cards.n: You must justify the minimum, not just report the time - a bare time value earns no justification credit.

cards.q: Pollutant enters a lake at rate E(t) tons/day and is removed at rate M(t) tons/day. If the amount at t = a is A, write an expression for the amount at t = b.
cards.a: Amount at t=b is A + $\int_a^b [E(t)-M(t)] dt$.
cards.h: → initial amount + integral of (entering rate − removal rate)
cards.n: This exact setup - integral of net rate - is the skeleton of every rate in/out FRQ; memorize the shape, not the numbers.

cards.q: For the pollutant model, explain how finding the total amount that entered the lake between t = a and t = b differs from finding the net change over that time.
cards.a: Total amount entered integrates only the entering rate: $\int_a^b E(t) dt$. Net change subtracts what left too: $\int_a^b [E(t)-M(t)] dt$. 'Total entered' ignores removal entirely.
cards.h: → 'total entered' integrates E(t) alone; net change integrates E(t) − M(t)
cards.n: Confusing these two quantities is a frequent misread of the question's wording.

cards.q: Cars enter a lot at E(t) = 5 + 4sin(t) per minute and leave at L(t) = 6 per minute for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, starting with 20 cars. Is the number of cars increasing at t = 4? Justify.
cards.a: E(4) - L(4) = 5 + 4sin(4) - 6 ≈ -4.03, which is negative, so the number of cars is decreasing (not increasing) at t = 4, because the exit rate exceeds the entry rate at that moment.
cards.h: → sign of E(t) − L(t) at t=4, then a sentence naming which rate is larger
cards.n: Answering 'no' correctly on an 'is it increasing' question is just as valid as answering 'yes.'

cards.q: A table gives f(2) = 5 and f(6) = 5, with f continuous and differentiable on [2,6]. Must there be a c in (2,6) with f'(c) = 0? Justify.
cards.a: Yes. f is continuous on [2,6] and differentiable on (2,6), and f(2)=f(6), so by the Mean Value Theorem there exists c in (2,6) with $f'(c) = \frac{f(6)-f(2)}{6-2} = 0$.
cards.h: → MVT with equal endpoint values gives f'(c) = 0
cards.n: This is Rolle's Theorem in disguise - readers accept the MVT justification with the difference quotient equal to 0.

cards.q: A table gives g(1) = -3 and g(4) = 2, with g continuous on [1,4]. Must there be a c in (1,4) with g(c) = 0? Justify.
cards.a: Yes. g is continuous on [1,4], and 0 is between g(1)=-3 and g(4)=2, so by the Intermediate Value Theorem there exists c in (1,4) with g(c) = 0.
cards.h: → IVT: continuity + 0 between the two given values
cards.n: State that 0 lies between the two given values explicitly - that comparison is the point, not just citing IVT by name.

cards.q: A table gives v(t) at t = 0, 2, 5, 9, 10 seconds. Use a trapezoidal sum over these four subintervals to approximate $\int_0^{10} v(t) dt$.
cards.a: Sum $\frac{1}{2}(t_2-t_1)(v_1+v_2)$ over each subinterval [0,2],[2,5],[5,9],[9,10] using the table's v values at each endpoint, then add the four pieces. Report the sum with correct distance units.
cards.h: → sum of (1/2)(width)(sum of two heights) over each unequal subinterval
cards.n: The subintervals here are unequal, so each trapezoid needs its own width - one averaged width is wrong.

cards.q: Explain why a trapezoidal sum built from a table of v(t) values may not equal the exact value of $\int_0^{10} v(t) dt$.
cards.a: The trapezoidal sum only uses the given data points and assumes v is linear between them. The true integral depends on v's actual behavior between those points, which the table does not show, so the sum is an approximation unless v truly is piecewise linear.
cards.h: → trapezoids assume linear behavior between the known points
cards.n: This explanation in words is often its own rubric point - do not skip it because the calculation is done.

cards.q: A table gives h'(x) at x = 0, 3, 5, 8 as 4, -1, -1, 3. Estimate h''(6) using the table, and explain what your answer represents.
cards.a: Approximate $h''(6) ≈ \frac{h'(8)-h'(5)}{8-5} = \frac{3-(-1)}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$. This estimates the instantaneous rate of change of h'(x) - the concavity of h - near x = 6, using the nearest surrounding table values.
cards.h: → difference quotient of the h' values bracketing x=6
cards.n: Use the two table points that straddle x = 6, not the two closest to 0.

cards.q: A table gives f(1) = 2 and f(5) = 2, but f is only known to be defined (not stated continuous or differentiable) on [1,5]. Can you conclude there is a c in (1,5) with f'(c) = 0? Explain.
cards.a: No. The Mean Value Theorem requires f to be continuous on [1,5] and differentiable on (1,5); without those hypotheses stated, the conclusion cannot be guaranteed even though the endpoint values are equal.
cards.h: → check that the hypotheses are actually given before applying the theorem
cards.n: This is a common trap: matching endpoint values alone is not enough without the continuity and differentiability hypotheses.

cards.q: The graph of f' (not f) is continuous, with f'(x) > 0 on (0,3), f'(x) < 0 on (3,6), and f'(3) = 0. Identify and justify any relative extrema of f on (0,6).
cards.a: f has a relative maximum at x = 3, because f'(x) changes from positive to negative at x = 3, satisfying the first derivative test.
cards.h: → read the sign change off the f' graph, apply the first derivative test
cards.n: Remember the graph shown is f', not f - reading rising/falling directly off the wrong curve is a common error.

cards.q: Given the same f' graph, f' is decreasing on (0,3) and increasing on (3,6). Identify any points of inflection of f, with justification.
cards.a: f has a point of inflection at x = 3, because f'' changes sign there: f' is decreasing before x = 3 (so f'' < 0) and increasing after (so f'' > 0).
cards.h: → where f' switches from decreasing to increasing, f'' changes sign
cards.n: Points of inflection come from where f' changes direction, not where f' equals 0.

cards.q: $f(x) = x^3-6x^2+9x+2$ on [0,5]. Find the absolute maximum value of f on this interval and justify it is the absolute maximum.
cards.a: $f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)$, critical points x = 1, 3. f(0)=2, f(1)=6, f(3)=2, f(5)=22. Comparing all candidates (critical points and endpoints), the absolute maximum is f(5)=22.
cards.h: → candidates test: critical points and both endpoints, compare all values
cards.n: The largest value here is at an endpoint, not a critical point - always check both endpoints on a closed interval.

cards.q: For $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+2$, find all intervals where f is concave up, with justification.
cards.a: f''(x) = 6x - 12, which is positive when x > 2. So f is concave up on (2,∞), because f''(x) > 0 there.
cards.h: → solve f''(x) > 0, then state the interval
cards.n: State the interval using the domain given in the problem if one was specified, not just the sign of f'' alone.

cards.q: Write the tangent line to $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+2$ at x = 1, and use it to approximate f(1.2).
cards.a: f(1)=6, f'(1)=0, so the tangent line is y = 6 + 0(x-1) = 6. The approximation is f(1.2) ≈ 6.
cards.h: → y = f(a) + f'(a)(x−a), then plug in the new x
cards.n: If asked, state over/underestimate using concavity - f is concave down near x=1, so this overestimates.

cards.q: Explain how to determine whether a linear approximation of f at x = a overestimates or underestimates f near a.
cards.a: If f is concave up near a (f''(a)>0), the tangent line lies below the curve, so the approximation underestimates f. If f is concave down (f''(a)<0), the tangent line lies above the curve, so it overestimates.
cards.h: → concave up → underestimate; concave down → overestimate
cards.n: This explanation needs the word 'concave' and a reason, not just 'because the graph curves.'

cards.q: Explain, using proper notation, what it means for f to be differentiable at x = a.
cards.a: $\lim_{h→0} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$ exists as a finite number. If it exists, it equals f'(a); if the left- and right-hand limits of this quotient differ, or the limit fails to exist, f is not differentiable at a.
cards.h: → the limit of the difference quotient as h→0 must exist
cards.n: This definition, not a graphical description, is what readers want when asked to explain differentiability.

cards.q: A particle moves along the x-axis with $v(t)=t^2-4t+3$ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 5. Find all times the particle changes direction, with justification.
cards.a: v(t)=(t-1)(t-3) changes sign at t = 1 and t = 3, both in [0,5], so the particle changes direction at both times - once positive to negative, once negative to positive - since a direction change requires velocity to change sign.
cards.h: → find where v(t) changes sign, state both times
cards.n: A particle changes direction where velocity changes sign, not merely where it equals zero.

cards.q: For the particle with $v(t)=t^2-4t+3$, find the total distance traveled from t = 0 to t = 5.
cards.a: Total distance = $\int_0^5 |v(t)| dt$, split at the direction changes t=1, t=3: $\int_0^1 v dt - \int_1^3 v dt + \int_3^5 v dt$. Evaluate each piece and add the absolute values for a positive total distance.
cards.h: → split the integral at direction changes, use |v(t)|
cards.n: Integrating v(t) directly over [0,5] gives net displacement, not total distance - these are graded as different quantities.

cards.q: A particle has position $x(t)=t^3-3t$. Find its speed at t = 2, and state whether it is speeding up or slowing down.
cards.a: $v(t)=3t^2-3$, so v(2)=9, speed = |v(2)| = 9. a(t)=6t, so a(2)=12. Since v(2) and a(2) share a sign (both positive), the particle is speeding up at t = 2.
cards.h: → speed = |v(t)|; speeding up when v and a share a sign
cards.n: Speed is always |v(t)|, never v(t) itself - a negative velocity still gives a positive speed.

cards.q: A curve is given by $x(t)=t^2-1$, $y(t)=t^3-3t$. Find dy/dx at t = 2.
cards.a: dx/dt=2t, $dy/dt=3t^2-3$. $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}=\frac{3t^2-3}{2t}$. At t=2: 9/4.
cards.n: Never divide dy by dx directly - both derivatives must be taken with respect to the parameter first.

cards.q: For $x(t)=t^2-1$, $y(t)=t^3-3t$, write an integral expression for the arc length from t = 0 to t = 2.
cards.a: Arc length = $\int_0^2 \sqrt{(dx/dt)^2+(dy/dt)^2} dt = \int_0^2 \sqrt{(2t)^2+(3t^2-3)^2} dt$. Leave unsimplified unless a decimal value is requested.
cards.h: → integral of √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt over the given bounds
cards.n: The setup with both derivatives squared under the root is the point - a decimal with no expression shown is not enough.

cards.q: For a particle with position x(t) and velocity v(t), state the condition on x(t) and v(t) that tells you the particle is moving away from the origin at time t.
cards.a: The particle moves away from the origin when x(t) and v(t) have the same sign at that time - position and velocity pointing the same direction mean distance from the origin is increasing.
cards.h: → x(t) and v(t) share a sign
cards.n: This is the same logic as speeding up/slowing down, applied to position and velocity instead of velocity and acceleration.

cards.q: An object moves with velocity v(t) = (3t, 2t-1) and position (2,5) at t = 0. Find the object's position at t = 3.
cards.h: → each coordinate is initial value + integral of that component of velocity
cards.n: Integrate each component of the velocity vector separately - do not combine them into one integral.

cards.q: A particle's position is $r(t) = (t^2, ln(t+1))$ for t ≥ 0. Find the particle's velocity vector and its speed at t = 1.
cards.h: → differentiate each component, then take the magnitude of the result
cards.n: Speed for a vector-valued function is the magnitude of the velocity vector, both components under one square root.

cards.q: For the polar curve r = 3 + 2cos(θ), write an integral expression for the area enclosed over 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π.
cards.a: Area = $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2π} [3+2cos(θ)]^2 dθ$. Leave the integrand unsimplified unless a decimal value is requested.
cards.n: Forgetting the factor of 1/2 in front of the integral is the most common error on polar area.

cards.q: For r = 3 + 2cos(θ), set up dy/dx at θ = π/2.
cards.a: x = r cos(θ), y = r sin(θ). dx/dθ = r'(θ)cos(θ) - r(θ)sin(θ), dy/dθ = r'(θ)sin(θ) + r(θ)cos(θ), with r'(θ) = -2sin(θ). Then dy/dx = (dy/dθ) ÷ (dx/dθ), evaluated at θ = π/2.
cards.h: → convert to x(θ), y(θ), then dy/dx = (dy/dθ) ÷ (dx/dθ)
cards.n: Polar dy/dx is graded as a parametric problem in disguise - never differentiate r with respect to θ and call it dy/dx.

cards.q: A slope field is shown for dy/dx = x - y. Describe how to sketch the solution curve through the point (0,2) using the field.
cards.a: Starting at (0,2), follow the direction of the segments shown at and near that point, moving through the field so the curve's slope at every point matches the field's segment there, extending smoothly in both directions.
cards.h: → start at the given point, follow the segments' slopes through the grid
cards.n: The curve must pass through the exact given point and match segment directions locally, not just have a plausible overall shape.

cards.q: Given dy/dx = x - y with y(0) = 2, use Euler's method with step size 0.5 to approximate y(1).
cards.h: → y_new = y_old + (step)(slope at old point), repeat
cards.n: Recompute the slope at each new point using the differential equation - do not reuse the first slope for every step.

cards.q: Solve the separable differential equation dy/dx = xy with y(0) = 3.
cards.a: Separate: (1/y) dy = x dx. Integrate: $ln|y|=\frac{x^2}{2}+C$. Use y(0)=3: ln 3 = C. So $ln|y|=\frac{x^2}{2}+ln 3$, giving $y=3e^{x^2/2}$.
cards.h: → separate variables, integrate both sides, solve for C, then solve for y
cards.n: Solving explicitly for y at the end is its own point - stopping at ln|y| = ... loses credit.

cards.q: A population P grows by dP/dt = 0.02P(1-P/500). State the carrying capacity and explain what it represents.
cards.a: The carrying capacity is 500, the nonzero value of P where dP/dt = 0. As t increases, P approaches 500 and growth slows toward zero, representing the maximum sustainable population in this model.
cards.h: → carrying capacity = the nonzero value that makes dP/dt = 0
cards.n: The carrying capacity is read directly from the (1 − P/L) factor - it is L, not the growth-rate constant 0.02.

cards.q: For dP/dt = 0.02P(1-P/500), find the value of P at which the population is growing fastest, with justification.
cards.a: The population grows fastest at P = 250, half the carrying capacity, because dP/dt as a function of P is a downward parabola in P, maximized at P = L/2 - the point of inflection of P(t).
cards.h: → fastest growth at P = L/2 (half the carrying capacity)
cards.n: This is a known result to state and justify, not something to rederive with calculus each time under time pressure.

cards.q: Explain why a slope field for dy/dx = x - y has horizontal segments only along a specific line, and identify that line.
cards.a: Segments are horizontal where dy/dx = 0, meaning x - y = 0, so along the line y = x. Every plotted segment on that line has slope 0.
cards.h: → set dy/dx = 0, solve for the relationship between x and y
cards.n: This kind of question is really asking you to solve dy/dx = 0 as an equation, not to describe the picture qualitatively.

cards.q: For dy/dx = x - y with slope 0 along y=x, positive slopes below that line, negative above, describe the solution through (2,0) and its long-run behavior.
cards.a: Starting at (2,0), below y=x, the slope is positive, so the curve rises; as it nears y=x its slope flattens toward 0, and the solution settles toward tracking close to the line y = x - 1 as x increases.
cards.h: → start point, direction nearby, behavior as it nears the slope-0 line
cards.n: Describing long-run behavior in words is often a separate rubric point from the sketch itself.

cards.q: Find the third-degree Taylor polynomial for $f(x)=e^x$ centered at x = 0.
cards.a: $P_3(x)=1+x+\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^3}{3!}=1+x+\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{6}$, since every derivative of $e^x$ at 0 equals 1.
cards.h: → sum of f^(k)(0) x^k / k! for k = 0 to 3
cards.n: Leaving the factorials in the denominator is accepted, but do not drop them.

cards.q: Using the known Maclaurin series for sin(x), write the first three nonzero terms of the Maclaurin series for sin(x^2).
cards.a: sin(x) = x − x^3/3! + x^5/5! − ⋯ (its Maclaurin series). Substituting x^2 for x: $sin(x^2) = x^2 - \frac{x^6}{6} + \frac{x^{10}}{120}$ (first three nonzero terms).
cards.h: → substitute x² into the known sin(x) series
cards.n: Substituting into a memorized series is almost always faster and safer than differentiating sin(x²) from scratch.

cards.q: Find the radius of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^{∞} \frac{(x-2)^n}{n×3^n}$.
cards.a: Ratio test: $\lim_{n→∞} |\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}|$ simplifies to $\frac{|x-2|}{3}$. This is less than 1 when |x-2| < 3, so the radius of convergence is 3.
cards.h: → ratio test, simplify to |x−2|/R < 1, read off R
cards.n: The radius is the number the ratio test's inequality compares |x − center| to - here it is 3, not 1/3.

cards.q: For the power series $\sum \frac{(x-2)^n}{n×3^n}$ with radius of convergence 3, test the endpoint x = -1 for convergence.
cards.a: At x=-1: $\sum \frac{(-3)^n}{n×3^n} = \sum \frac{(-1)^n}{n}$, which converges by the Alternating Series Test (terms alternate, |1/n| decreases to 0). So x = -1 is included.
cards.h: → substitute the endpoint, identify the resulting series, apply the matching test
cards.n: Each endpoint needs its own test - the ratio test is always inconclusive exactly at the endpoints.

cards.q: For $\sum \frac{(x-2)^n}{n×3^n}$ with radius of convergence 3, test the endpoint x = 5 for convergence, and state the full interval.
cards.a: At x=5: $\sum \frac{3^n}{n×3^n}=\sum\frac{1}{n}$, the harmonic series, which diverges. So x = 5 is excluded. Combined with the other endpoint, the interval of convergence is [-1,5).
cards.h: → substitute the endpoint, recognize the harmonic series, then state the full interval
cards.n: State the complete interval at the end, combining both endpoint results - that combined statement is often its own point.

cards.q: The 4th-degree Taylor polynomial for f about x = 1 approximates f(1.2). Given |f^(5)(x)| ≤ 6 on [1,1.2], bound the error.
cards.a: By the Lagrange error bound, $|R_4(1.2)| ≤ \frac{6×(0.2)^5}{5!} = \frac{6×0.00032}{120} = 0.000016$. The approximation is within 0.000016 of the true value.
cards.n: n is the degree of the polynomial, so the exponent and factorial use n+1 = 5, not 4.

cards.q: A series is alternating with terms decreasing to 0. Its fourth partial sum S4 approximates the sum. Bound the error in this approximation.
cards.a: By the Alternating Series Error Bound, the error is at most $|a_5|$, the absolute value of the first omitted term, since the series meets the alternating series test conditions.
cards.h: → error ≤ absolute value of the first omitted term
cards.n: This bound only applies once you've confirmed the series satisfies the alternating series test - state that first.

cards.q: Write the Maclaurin series for 1/(1-x) in sum notation, and use it to write the series for 1/(1-x^2).
cards.a: $\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{∞} x^n$ for |x|<1. Substituting x^2 for x: $\frac{1}{1-x^2}=\sum_{n=0}^{∞} x^{2n}$ for |x|<1.
cards.h: → start from the geometric series, substitute x² for x
cards.n: Recognizing 1/(1−x²) as the geometric series in disguise is faster than any direct Taylor computation.

cards.q: Determine whether $\int_1^{∞} \frac{1}{x^2} dx$ converges, and find its value if it does.
cards.a: $\int_1^{∞} \frac{1}{x^2} dx = \lim_{b→∞} \int_1^b x^{-2} dx$. Evaluating: $\lim_{b→∞} (1-\frac{1}{b}) = 1$. The integral converges to 1.
cards.h: → replace ∞ with b, take the limit as b→∞ after integrating
cards.n: The limit notation itself is graded - jumping straight to a numeric answer without the limit step loses the setup point.

cards.q: Determine whether $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} dx$ converges, using the limit definition to justify.
cards.a: $\int_0^1 \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} dx = \lim_{a→0} \int_a^1 x^{-1/2} dx$ (a approaching 0 from the right). Evaluating: $\lim_{a→0}(2-2\sqrt{a})=2$. It converges because the limit exists and is finite.
cards.h: → limit as a→0 from the right, since the discontinuity is at x=0
cards.n: This integral is improper because the integrand is undefined at x = 0, not because a bound is infinite.

cards.q: State what changed about AP Calculus BC Section I (multiple choice) for May 2027.
cards.a: Multiple choice is now 42 questions in 1 hour 40 minutes, still 50% of the score — down from 45 questions in 1 hour 45 minutes. The split is Part A 29 questions in 62 minutes with no calculator, Part B 13 questions in 38 minutes with a graphing calculator required.
cards.h: → 42 questions, 1:40 total, 50%; per-part split not fixed here
cards.n: Most Calc BC prep material published before 2027 still says 45 questions and 1 hour 45 minutes, split 30/15 — none of those four numbers matches your exam.

cards.q: State what did not change about AP Calculus BC Section II (free response) for May 2027.
cards.a: Free response is unchanged: 6 questions in 1 hour 30 minutes, worth 50% of the score, with a calculator-required part and a no-calculator part.
cards.n: Every FRQ rubric rule, pacing habit, and content skill you practice from an older book still applies - only the MC section's numbers changed.

cards.q: Explain how the total AP Calculus BC testing time changed for May 2027.
cards.a: Multiple choice dropped from 1 hour 45 minutes to 1 hour 40 minutes, while free response stayed at 1 hour 30 minutes, so total testing time is now 3 hours 10 minutes instead of 3 hours 15 minutes.
cards.h: → MC time drops 5 minutes; total time drops from 3:15 to 3:10
cards.n: The 5 fewer minutes come entirely out of the MC section - FRQ pacing is untouched.

cards.q: Explain how an older prep book's MC breakdown (30 questions/60 minutes, 15 questions/45 minutes) differs from the May 2027 exam.
cards.a: Those numbers summed to the old total of 45 questions in 105 minutes. May 2027 is 42 questions in 100 minutes, split 29 questions in 62 minutes with no calculator and 13 questions in 38 minutes with a calculator — so the no-calculator part gained two minutes while the calculator part lost seven, and both lost questions.
cards.h: → old split summed to 45/105; new total is 42/100, so it can't just carry over
cards.n: The cut was not spread evenly: Part B lost two questions and seven minutes, Part A lost one question and gained two minutes.

cards.q: State the numbers to pace AP Calculus BC Section I by for May 2027.
cards.a: 42 questions in 1 hour 40 minutes overall, about 2 minutes 23 seconds each. Part A is 29 questions in 62 minutes with no calculator, about 2 minutes 8 seconds each; Part B is 13 questions in 38 minutes with a graphing calculator, about 2 minutes 55 seconds each.
cards.h: → certain: 42 q / 100 min overall; uncertain: the per-part split
cards.n: Pace each part against its own clock, not the overall average — Part A runs 15 seconds a question tighter than the average suggests.
